speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege: I have just been presiding over a meeting of the coordinating committee of the dominion-provincial conference and have left its proceedings in order to make a statement to the house immediately in respect to a very misleading article which appears in the Ottawa morning Journal of to-day. The entire membership of the conference took strong exception to this article and desired that I should make a statement to the House of Commons . on behalf of all who are present at the conference.
The article is entitled: "Cabinet clash complicates conference. No announcements made after second session." It reads:
When the coordinating committee of the dominion-provincial conference reached the end of another session last night with no public announcements from Prime Minister King, it was confirmed by some of those leaving the chamber that two paramount issues seemed to be complicating deliberations.
They were:
1.	Reports confirmed by several provincial premiers of disagreement among Prime Minister King and two of his colleagues;
2.	Determination, not unexpected, of the nine provincial premiers to make not the slightest retreat from their stand on provincial rights.
A little further on in the article it says:
On the point of disagreement among the dominion ministers, it was described by the provincial men as "a clash".
May I say that all provincial premiers and all members of the dominion government who were present at the conference are united in saying that, they know nothing of a clash having taken place between myself and any of my colleagues. As a matter of fact there has been nothing of the kind. I make that statement emphatically. May I add that there has been nothing that I am aware of, and that I think any of the premiers on the coordinating committee are aware of, which has in any way complicated the proceedings that have been, 47696-163J
I am happy to say, going forward so amicably and splendidly since the opening of the conference.
I am authorized to make this statement by the entire group that are to-day discussing these dominion-provincial questions, and discussing them, I think, in an exceptionally able and amicable manner.
Until the committee of the conference concludes its proceedings no statement will be given out. When a statement is given out it is one that will be approved by the entire conference. I hope, therefore, that so far as the public of Canada are concerned they will draw their inferences with respect to the proceedings of the conference from the official statement which may be issued by the conference itself when it has concluded its proceedings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have the permission of the house to make a statement with regard to a question asked this morning. I was not in the house this morning when the leader of the opposition asked about a letter I had sent to the President of the United States suggesting the desirability of consultation between our two governments before a final decision was made in the United States on the discontinuance of meat rationing. I was not aware of the considerations which compelled immediate action by the United States authorities, and had prepared a message to the President on the assumption that it might be possible to arrange for further discussion on this very complex and difficult problem.
As I explained in my statement to the house on Friday afternoon, 'there are fundamental differences between the problems of control confronting a' country like the United States which normally exports some five per cent of its meat production and those in a country like Canada where thirty per cent to forty per cent of output finds its way into export markets. Both governments have made commitments to allied and liberated countries where the average level of food consumption is very much lower than on this continent. Both countries are determined to carry out these promises, though methods and arrangements by which they implement them will naturally differ.
Since my suggestion to the President was, in fact, received too late for consideration, and since the position of our own government was made clear to the house at the first opportunity, I do not think there is any purpose in my taking up at this stage with President Truman the question of our making public the actual texts of the messages exchanged.

When he replies I should like him to tell us if anything has been done to protect our cattle market to the south. During the war I refrained from saying very much about it. From speaking to the minister and to other people I know in the government service, I know the position well. The Minister of Reconstruction said the other night that the government policy had been one of protecting export markets. I believe that statement was made in connection with lumber, when it was pointed out that we had sent overseas about forty or fifty per cent of our cut. I am wondering what protection there is, or what arrangements the minister through his department has made for the continuation of those 297,000 head of cattle to the United States in the four quarters, which were a boon to western farmers.
I have given a good deal of thought to the overseas market, and sometimes I wonder if we shall be able to hold it. We see the magnificent progress Denmark is making in retaining her bacon market. Realizing that ws are so far away from the market, we must understand that we shall find it difficult to compete, even if we produce the same grades as they do. My belief is that our bacon is just as good as that of Denmark. The difficulty is that Denmark is prepared to take so much in exchange from Great Britain which we shall not be able to take.
A couple of years ago when Lord Delaware was in the city of Quebec he was asked about our retaining the British market, and his reply was, "Well, what will you take from us?" We have developed great numbers of mechanics. We do not want to buy engines or bicycles from Great Britain. But if we expect them to take our cattle and hogs we must be prepared to buy from them. The Argentine can produce cattle more economically and of just as good quality as we can. It costs the western farmer just as much to ship his beef from Calgary to Montreal as it costs the Argentine farmer to ship to Smithfield, Liverpool, or Glasgow. We are up against a difficult problem.

The rail grading of hogs is all right, but the difficulty is that it is so definitely 'in the hands of the - packers. The minister would have eighty per cent of the farmers behind him if he were to set u,p a board of live stock commissioners. If he does not give them that, then they are going to ask for the nationalization of the packing industry; there is -nothing else for it. If the hon. member will read my speech he will see that in no single instance was I advocating any such prices. I was attempting to denounce .the constant grumbling of western members of parliament that I have listened to for so many years.

I would point out that so long as we have members spreading false ideas regarding western Canada, such as the hon. member has spread, then there will be complaints in western Canada. Early in the fall the government advertised throughout western Canada advising the farmers to ship their cattle as early as possible because there would probably be a heavy run on the market in October and November. I think the government were well advised in doing that, especially in those areas where there was a shortage of feed. Unfortunately in many parts of the drought area a serious situation has developed because farmers miscalculated. As the minister knows, winter came on quite early; snow came in October, and farmers had to start feeding in that month whereas they ordinarily would not have to start feeding until the first of the month. As a result of this situation a serious shortage of feed, has developed in those areas. The farmers are finding it difficult, as the government prophesied, to dispose of their cattle at this time.
I should like to ask the minister what their survey shows the situation to be in the drought areas of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I should like to know how great the shortage of feed will be, how. much feed will have to be shipped into those areas, or on the other hand how much stock will have to be shipped out in order to avoid a heavy loss of cattle.

I realize that this situation is dealt with jointly by the provincial and federal governments, but no doubt the minister has a clear picture of the whole situation.

Before this battle of Bannockburn is ended, I should like to say just a word or two with respect to the whole situation, arising partly from the unwise remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). The other night that gentleman did Alberta and the west a greater disservice than any man coming from western Canada has ever done since I came' to this house in 1935. He conveyed the idea that conditions in the west were far better than they actually are. The hon. member named the finest area in Alberta as an example of one in which men were not broke, but he chose to overlook entirely the area surrounding Medicine Hat, where drought conditions prevail so frequently, and he overlooked entirely the area the hon. member for Acadia represents and many other areas in Alberta where crop failures are almost common. If the hon. member had informed himself better concerning conditions in Alberta and the west generally before rushing into Hansard with a speech which would mislead men like the hon. member for Renfrew North, it would have been much better for everybody from the west.
Incidentally let me point out to the hon. member for Renfrew North-I think he had me in mind as one of the' grumblers-that since I came here I have endeavoured to set forth the true conditions in the west.
There are three things which should be considered before attempting to form a correct estimate of conditions in the west. The first is the freight rate situation. If the hon. member has listened to what has been said by members from the west he will have heard that discussed many times. When the hon. member can explain why in the Dominion of Canada a condition obtains under which a man can put one hundred pounds of barbed wire on the train at Montreal and ship it to Vancouver for seventy-five cents, but when he takes that hundred pounds of wire off at Edmonton he has to pay $1.98, he will be doing something to explain the painful incidence of a situation such as this on the agricultural communities of Manitoba, Saskatche-. wan and Alberta. He will then be in a far better position to be fair in his judgment of the wmst. This adverse freight situation is one of the greatest grievances we have in the west, and no amount of comment, no amount of complaint, no amount.of pleading which western members can bring to bear on the men
Supply-Agriculture

in Ottawa, can cause the slightest deviation from the destructive policy which has obtained in this country for generations.
This is a situation which literally bleeds the farmers of the west to death. Not only do they suffer from the adverse freight rate on freight shipped out to the west; they suffer from an adverse freight rate on freight which they ship to the east. Evidence can be brought to show that through the freight rate structure the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have erected a tariff wall against the products of the secondary industries which are based on agricultural products and are located in western Canada. This is a condition which cries to high heaven, but do you think that all the members from the west pleading about this matter can even phase the men from Ontario and Quebec? Up to the present time it has been utterly impossible even to get ourselves heard at all. There is a situation which the hon. member for Renfrew North, being a public spirited man-I give him credit for that-should give close attention to; certainly before he makes any remark such as he made last night he should carefully weigh these things.
There is another serious matter. The tariff incidence is a scandal. The tariff has been arranged so that it protects the producers of Ontario and Quebec and militates against the producers in every other one of the seven provinces of Canada, both east and west.
You did not say anything about the maritimes.

I said all the other provinces, east or west. The situation is just as serious for the maritimes as it is for the west. The maritimes are unable to have their voice heard in the slightest degree. Let me illustrate by giving some figures from memory, although I think my recollection is correct. In one of the thirties, I believe 1931, an investigation was carried on under the direction of the late Hon. Norman McLeod Rogers, who was minister of labour in the federal government from 1935 until he became minister of national defence snd later lost his life. The discoveries of that investigation were to the effect that Alberta paid $19,000,000 per year in enhanced prices arising out of the tariff more than she obtained by way of protection. In the same year Saskatchewan paid $25,000,000 per year more in enhanced prices than she obtained by way of protection through the tariff. At the same time the producers of Ontario received protection to the extent of $51,000,000 a year more than they paid, and th^ producers of the province of Quebec received protection to the extent

of $31,000,000 a year more than they paid. Now this is a situation which I am sure even the hon. member for Renfrew North will recognize as being iniquitous, a situation which should have been taken care of long ago. Has even the slightest attention been given to the matter by the people in charge of the government of Canada? Not the slightest bit; and, generally speaking, when members from the west rise and begin to talk they are accused' of "whining" and all that sort of thing, just, as the hon. member did last night; or, hon. members for Ontario and Quebec just get up and "hulk" out of the house, and, leave the members from the west or the members from the east to talk. The time must come and come very soon when more attention shall be given to equity throughout this country than has been given to it up to the present time.
Another exxceedingly serious matter-it has been referred to by the hon. member for Selkirk-is the matter of the Palliser triangle. Many hon. members in the house at the present time are new here. For their sakes let me point out that in western Canada there is a vast area of country included in what is called the Palliser triangle. This whole area receives from year to year too little moisture to enable the producer there to produce on a basis which will guarantee anything like security of tenure on the land. This situation was pointed out by Palliser many years ago. He said in a report to t-he government of those days that it would be unwise to permit settlement to take place on any extensive scale within the Palliser triangle. Now, the Palliser triangle includes such areas as, for example, the Medicine Hat and Acadia districts andl considerable parts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Notwithstanding the advice which was given-and it was sound advice-the dominion government authorities permitted settlers to come in in vast numbers and settle over those areas without knowing what conditions they were running into. In those areas you will find, probably, that one year there will be sufficient rainfall, and you might think you had come to paradise itself. The next year you will perhaps find that the whole country is just a dust-bowl. -Crop failures will go on as long as, say, three years, and then will come a good year, with crops such as the hon. member for Renfrew North saw, and people will say, "surely it must be little short of a paradise1; they are rolling in wealth." But if the hon. member had stayed there three or four years, or had lived in these districts over a period of fifteen years, he would know a good deal more about conditions in the west.

Coming back to the question of settling this area, the dominion government allowed people to settle all over the region of the Palliser triangle; in, fact, they encouraged them with examples of glowing propaganda, inviting them to come to Canada, and picturing the conditions in the good years, until people settled there by the tens of thousands. What happened? Very soon these people needed, roads, schools, telephones and many other services. All of these cost money. Who had to bear the expense of building the roads, of establishing and maintaining the schools, or erecting the telephone lines? The provincial governments. The dominion government brought people in here and settled them on the land, thus building up an impossible problem for 'the provincial governments, and then backed gracefully out of the picture, and under the inspiration of such men as the hon. member for Renfrew North, whose lack of information regarding the whole situation is colossal, they began immediately to accuse the provinces of poor management; they wondered1 why they went into debt, and all that sort of thing.
That condition still exists. Not only was the settlement of the Palliser triangle a colossal blunder at the time; not only did it constitute an insupportable burden on the shoulders of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta particularly, but other settlement problems resulted from dominion policy. One of these arose out of the plan under which the dominion granted the Canadian Pacific Railway company and the Hudson's Bay company vast stretches of country selected by them wherever they chose to select it. It did not matter a particle whether communities were established alongside the areas selected -by the Hudson's Bay company and the CfP.R. The whole settlement of the country was spread out over a wide area, rendering it necessary to build far more miles of railroad, to erect far more lines of telephones, to establish far more schools for the children: in widely settled areas, and, more recently, far more costly health and dental services. All this has constituted a drain on the provincial authorities of which hon. members from Ontario and Quebec have not remotely dreamed. But these prairie provinces are expected to stand up under the strain, and they are condemned because they falter or stagger under this insupportable burden.	.
Now, when hon. members get up in the house and inform the hon. member for Renfrew North and other members form Ontario and Quebec, in the vain hope that probably some day attention will be paid to their problems and redress will be made, these members
have to Stand under the condemnation of sweeping remarks such as we had to endure here last night. That is a condition which I certainly hope will not be revealed in the house again. Then we have had the hon. member for Calgary West come down and in a short speech convey an absolutely false impression of the whole set-up. Not a word did the hon. member say about the freight rate structure, although he must know it exists. Not a word did he say about the adverse tariff, although he must know it exists. Not a word did he undertake to say about the Palliser triangle and all the evils which have resulted in the west from that situation. He simply left all the people throughout Canada open to the misinterpretation and misinformation which would naturally result from speeches such as the hon. member for Renfrew North gave.
I do not desire to occupy any more of the time of the committee just now, but I felt that I should have been remiss, in my duty to western Canada, remiss in my duty to Ontario and Quebec, which do not desire that there shall be inequity in this country, and remiss in my duty to all other parts of Canada, if I omitted to rise and make clear to some extent the situation which obtains in Canada, as a result of which this condition of inequity has arisen as between the various provinces of this great dominion.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to enter 'this battle, which might be known as another battle of Bannockburn. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) acquitted himself, I think, very well, and does not need my assistance. But I have a few observations to make, and nobody in this chamber will accuse me of taking very much of the time of the house, because I have made but one speech since I arrived here. Being a new member, I thought probably I was well advised not to say too much at the beginning; I have learned a good deal since I arrived, and, having been a student all my life, I feel satisfied that some of what I have learned was good. .
I want to refer particularly to a remark made by the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Cake) in his speech yesterday, when he said he deplored the drift of the young people from the farms. I heartily agree with what the hon. member for Grey North stated on that occasion. There is a very serious drift in this country from rural areas to urban centres, and it has been going on for decades. I am particularly concerned about the young folk, and I feel, with him, some apprehension that our whole economy is being gravely disturbed through the number of young people who are
Supply-Agriculture

leaving farm life and are going into urban centres to seek a living. It is not a satisfactory state of affairs, and there must be some definite reason for it.
Away back in 1871, according to the Canada Year Book, 80-42 per cent of our people lived in rural areas and only 19-58 in urban centres. Forty years later, in 1911, 54-58 peT cent lived in rural areas and 45~42 per cent in urban areas. In 1941, the last figures I have been able to obtain, ,we find that situation reversed, and now we have more people living in urban areas than in rural. In rural areas in 1941 there were 45-66 per cent and in urban areas 54-34. Everyone knows that since the war that drift has been definitely accelerated and it is not, as the hon. member suggested, due to the fact that labour conditions are better in the city than on the farms. That is not the whole reason. We know that power machinery on our farms is now lessening the hours of labour. I agree with all those who say that the hours of labour are still too long on the farm. But the fundamental reason, as I see it, is that farming is still on the whole unprofitable andi unattractive. That is borne out by the fact that although we have 450,000 discharged from the armed services, the director of the Department of Veterans Affairs, who is -in charge of the administration of the Veterans' Land Act, te-lls us that the greatest number of applications for farm land they can anticipate by the end of 1946 is 14,276, and by 1946 I suggest the bulk of our overseas personnel will be back home and discharged. That is much less than after the last war. Under the old soldier settlement act we settled 25,000 veterans, but we have not for-gottsn that of those 25,000 soldier settlers, owing largely to the vicissitudes of farm life, 13,000 abandoned their projects. They did not abandon those projects without some reason; they did- so because life on the farm was neither profitable nor attractive. That is the main reason. Farming must be made profitable, and I would commend the minister for anything he has done to set floor prices under farm products, regardless of what they are, whether wheat, butter, or any other farm product. I suggest that -while floor prices are all very well as far as they go, they do not go far enough, for the good reason that as long as farmers have to pay exorbitant prices for clothing, fuel or machinery, it stands to * reason that floor prices will not solve their problems. Floor prices did not solve their problems in 1934, because, of course, they did not exist then under the Conservative administration. According to the report submitted by the Rowell commission, at page 175, the farmer in that year was receiving $18 a head for his

cattle in Saskatchewan, 17 cents a pound for butter, 1(H cents a dozen for eggs, 61^ cents per bushel for wheat. I submit that $1 or S1.25 per bushel for wheat will be inadequate if the farmer still has to pay exorbitant prices as the result of tariffs or freight rates or monopoly control of most of the things he must buy.
Power farming to-day is most common east and west. The farmer owns a tractor, a truck, a combine and a plow. According to .the cartel report submitted in this house recently we know that monopolies exist. We are not talking about something that is not wholly familiar to most of the people of Canada. And the excessive prices that the farmer pays for many of the goods he purchases to-day are not due to labour costs. I have in my hand a report which any member may get by writing to the United States federal trade commissioner. It was issued in AVashington in 1945, so that it is up to date. According to this report a combine was marketed in the city of Minneapolis and sold for $638 retail. In the production of that combine, material costs amounted to $174.27; factory overhead, $93.07; manufacturer's discount, $57.96; manufacturer's margin, $85.77; dealer's discount for cash, $30.50; retail dealer's margin, $122; freight, $28 and labour, $46.43, or 7-3 per cent of the -retail price. That figure is not foreign- to many of us because in 1938 an inquiry was held here and many old members are familiar with some of the facts revealed on- that occasion. An eight-foot binder marketed -in Regina sold for $218, and the labour costs amounted to $22.63 or about 10i per cent.
Now, farm life lags behind city life not only in physical comforts but also in social, health and entertainment facilities, and in order to provide many of those things a satisfactory income is necessary. It is necessary in order to keep these services functioning and to create new ones. Farming can be made more attractive by the electrification of rural areas, because farm life is most laborious, particularly for the farm wife. If she is free to use electric power, if she has washing machines, frigidaire, a heating system, her work can be made much easier. And not only that; life may be made more -attractive for her and for the young people by the addition of lights, radio and all the things that can be provided by electrical power. The electrification inquiry commission- of Manitoba made this statement in 1942:
The electricfication of farm areas merits high priority as a post-war employment programme because it will be more nearly self-supporting *than most other projects which might be considered.

According to the Canada year book 19-8 per cent of the farms in Canada are electrified. In the United States, a country similar to our own, 38-6 per cent of the farms are electrified. That is double the number in Canada. I submit that in the post-war period the government should establish parity prices for farm products so that farming may be and continue to be profitable, and secondly that farm life be made more attractive by the provision of electrification for rural areas throughout the dominion.

As one who lived for a number of years in western Canada I remember the time when my father owned some sections of land in the Melfort area. From what I hear, my hon. friend has not studied the situation very well. The farmers are enjoying some prosperity out' there. The days of slavery are over in the Dominion of Canada. A man lives where he wants to live. There is no compulsion on any person to move from the east to the west or vice versa. One does not have to move from Ontario and Quebec and live on the prairies. We live in this country where we want to live, because it is the part of the country we like. I resent the aspersions that have been cast by several members of this house on the mental attitude of the easterner toward the westerner. I want to correct that. There is no group of people who are more pleased to see the west prosper than the citizens of Ontario and. Quebec. We all have taken trips, or we should have, to see this great country of ours, and when we go into the various parts of Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Manitoba we see progress. There is no group of people more delighted than we are when we see that, because it is our Canada as well as yours. None of us is correct in his assumptions of conditions existing in Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan or any other province in Canada. We can only be guided by the information we receive.
To hear some members from the east and from the west talk one would think that the United States was a land of milk and honey. I have had the unfortunate experience of travelling through Kansas, Missouri, and different parts of that country, and I have watched cattle standing on the hoof dying for want of proper food and water. I say to western members on all sides of the house that ninety per cent of the eastern people will do everything in their power to make the west prosperous. We do not want to hide behind unnecessary tariffs; we do not request that you people pay high freight rates. We are here as a group of men in parliament to see
that those difficulties are ironed out for the benefit of this country. Unless all provinces prosper, no one province or three provinces can prosper. I do not think it is right that any hon. member should be too emphatic in his statements wfith regard to one province or one section of this country. We are searching for unity. We have the greatest country in the world. Let us pull together and stop this battle of Bannockburn.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.

Is the hon. gentleman
speaking for his party when be says he is ready to do away with discriminatory freight rates and bring in a reduction of tariff items?

I have no right to speak for my party, but I will say this: I cannot understand my worthy leader not advocating that discriminatory freight rates -be dispensed with if it would be for the benefit of Canada. I am sure he would be backed a hundred per cent in dispensing with discriminatory rates. I know I would back him.

I feel I am compelled to take a moment or so of the committee's time because of something that was said about me by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). I appreciate his kindness in nominating me as having made the most harmful speech to the west in the last ten years, because I know occasionally it is better to have a bad record than no record at all. But in this particular case I did not hold it long. He took it away from ime within forty-eight hours, after I had it for twenty-four. I want to say this because I am sure he would not want the impression to go abroad that intentionally I am doing or saying anything harmful to the agriculturists in our country. He did say, for example, that I failed to mention the situation in the neighbourhood of the city of Medicine Hat. Well, if he will take the trouble to look at Hansard of the day before yesterday-I cannot recall the page at the moment-he will find that I said exactly what he did, that the Palliser triangle should not have been settled. If I did the west harm in saying that, then, of course, my hon. friend is in team harness with me and we are doing a very good heel-and-toe down that road.
He mentioned freight rates, and said that I had failed to mention them. I failed to do so because I did not think it was pertinent to this debate. That is the reason I did not

do it; but I am going to tell him something about freight rates that probably he does not know.
I shall be glad to hear it.
You will if you listen, but if you keep shouting you cannot hear it.
The hon. member's trouble is that he does not listen closely enough.

Yes. I enjoy a tete-a-tete, but I should like to hear what the other fellow is saying. I did not hear it, therefore I shall go on. With respect to freight rates, there is no question that. Alberta stands at the top of the heap. I have no doubt whatever that, freight rates, and our whole structure, require a going over. I think the time has long since come when our whole freight, structure should be based not on what the traffic will bear, but on the cost of doing the job. Hon, members know that they are rapidly coming to that in the United States. In the last couple of years the interstate commerce commission have issued1 new orders based on cost, which is not true of this country. I am going to let the hon. member know something more about freight rates. In Alberta we have a subvention paid to the railways for carrying Alberta coal. The hon. member for Calgary West got this subvention from the' dominion government. Perhaps the hon. menjber did not know that some years ago the hon. member for Calgary West appeared before the board of railway commissioners on behalf of the province of Alberta. The meeting lasted a week and an effort was made by the member for Calgary West to convince the board that the cost of hauling coal from his own area in Lethbridge to North Bay and to the city of Toronto was less than $8. In that I failed, but I am anxious that the hon. member should know that while he has been doing all the talking about these things the member for Calgary West has some little accomplishment to. his credit.
May I just say a word with respect to that?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Swift Current.

Mr. Chairman, like one of the previous speakers of our group I have not taken up much of the time of the house, but I wish to speak for a few moments now because I know of no other item under which I may be able to bring to the attention of the committee a. few of the things I am thinking about in connection with the matter under discussion. I am glad the last two speakers came out and made the statements which they did, that they, believe in unity andi that there were many things in the west which could be corrected. I cannot agree with hon. members who have suggested that there should have been no settlement in the Palliser triangle. There was a great deal of splendid land in that section. I will agree that there are some places in the Palliser triangle which should never have been settled. I agree that the responsibility rests on the dominion government of that time for allowing and encouraging settlement to take place there. I agree with the method that is being applied now. in all too minor a way, to correct some of these things through the dominion government in the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Some of these things are in the process of being corrected. I wish the house would vote the Minister of Agriculture three or four billion dollars so that he could do it all in one year, but I will not suggest that because it cannot be done. When we come to that item I am going to suggest that certainly more than two million dollars should be granted [DOT] for that work.
I was a little bit concerned the other night when the hon. member for Fort William made the remarks he did about how hard the farmers in his constituency have to work. He did not need to tell us that. All farmers in all constituencies of Canada work hard, and their wives work hard. In this connection I hope the Minister of Finance wall remember that the work done by a farm wife is a contribution to the productive power of this countiy. If the labourer is worthy of her hire, then she should have some compensation in the way of income instead of being classed as a housewife, with no occupation; regarded as more or less an appendage of her husband, while her husband is given a slight reduction in his income tax on that account.
I am glad to know there is not a lazy farmer in Canada.

I should not. like to say there are no lazy farmers in Canada. Judging by the empty seats in this chamber there may even be some lazy members of parliament, but. I would say most farmers who have been

Supply-Agriculture
on the land for a good many years cannot be very lazy or they would not have been able to stay on the land. If some of those going on farms to-day are lazy, they will not remain on the farms very long. I am talking about productive farms,' which make it possible for the railways to earn revenue by hauling freight; which make it possible for the commercial life of this country to be carried on. I am not talking of people who squat on a piece of land and live there with a cow, a pig and a hen and call themselves farmers. Some other method will have to be adopted to take care of them. I am talking about, the farmers who work, whether in my constituency or in that of the hon. member for Fort William. I am not bragging about them because they like to work, but they want a square deal in return.
I am very glad some things have been said in this discussion, because after listening to the hon. member for Fort William and the hon. member for Renfrew North I became rather concerned. When they were speaking, particularly the hon. member for Renfrew North, I began to wonder if that was the consensus of opinion of the citizens of Ontario and Quebec, and I thought if it was, there was only one thing for them to do. I would regret having them do it; but if the people in the east really felt that way, the only thing left would be for them to say to the poor relations in western Canada, "We are tired of you now. We are going to draw a line at the western border of eastern Canada and let you guys paddle your own canoe." We would not like to have that happen, because many of us have relatives and friends down here; our sentiments and emotions are tied up with the older provinces of Canada, and we passionately wrant to have unity in this dominion. But if it is going to be reduced to a purely economic question I can assure you we are quite capable of running our own show in western Canada if that is the way you feel about it. I hope not many hon. members or* citizens of the east feel that way. Certainly we do not.
As proof of the fact that we are prepared to conduct our own affairs, the hon. member for Churchill and the hon. member for Saskatoon City pointed out in a previous discussion in this house that the three prairie provinces would like to control and operate the port of Churchill and the Hudson Bay railway on their own behalf. It is the^ people down east who do not want that to be done. The minute the dominion government says to the western provinces, "Set up your board of management and take it over," they will find us more than willing to accept that responsibility,
because we know it can be operated. We are not impressed by the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply that the port of Churchill can operate only for about two months in the year; and when someone said, "Oh, oh," he replied that perhaps it could be operated for three months. We are quite convinced that it can operate for five or six months every year. We are able to read the history of mercantile navigation just as the minister can. Many of our people have visited Churchill, as the minister has, and we of the west are quite prepared to undertake the operation of that port just as soon as the government will give us the privilege of doing so. If they cannot find ways of getting ships into and out of that port with cargoes, we can.
I should like to remind the Minister of Trade and Commerce also that if this situation ever did occur, we would immediately establish contact with the big cooperative societies in the old country, who already have indicated to us that they want a great many of our products and are willing to bring us the things we want, which at present, because of the tariff arrangements of the dominion government, we cannot get through Montreal, Quebec, Saint John or Halifax. In this connection I should like to remind the government that some of our Saskatchewan people visited the old country last winter, less than a year ago. During a visit to our trade commissioner over there he was asked if he had made any effort to establish direct and close contact with the big English and Scottish cooperative wholesale societies, and his reply was, "No. I have been to their offices but I do not know very much about them." Give us the "right to operate Churchill and we will learn all about them, because we will visit them and establish relations.
I suggest to hon. members that if they get tired, as I expect they do, of hearing the representations made by western members, they might just give some indication of wanting to meet us on these grounds, and we shall be tickled to death to shut up. We do not love coming down here bringing our grievances, Mr. Chairman, bu't I always understood parliament was a place where the people from the various sections of the country might lay their grievances before those whom we presume to be broadminded, public-spirited men from all over the dominion, and where some redress for these grievances may be obtained. We want these things.
I should like to remind the hon. member for Renfrew North that the long-time average for the prairie provinces in the matter of grain production, both inside and outside the Pal-liser triangle, is about fifteen bushels to the
Supply-*Agriculture

acre. We cannot live for four or five years, waiting for good crops, without eating and without wearing clothes. We have to make the good years carry us through the bad. So that average of about fifteen bushels to the acre is what we consider it is possible to sell from the wheat producing areas of our country. As I painted out some time ago in the house, with an average of 20,000,000 aeres under cultivation that means from 280,000,000 to 300,000,000 bushels of wheat to be sold every year. We do not know what the future is going to bring us; we cannot make any predictions. We cannot even get men in high positions to give us accurate predictions. I have newspaper accounts here of statements made by two very able men closely associated with the production and marketing of wheat; yet if they are correctly reported their statements are completely at variance. The Minister of Agriculture is reported to have stated to the annual general meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates in the early part of this month that he did not believe it likely that the price of wheat would drop below $1.25 for the next five years.
No, that was not it. Read it. I did not say it was not likely; I said I did not know of anything at present that would bring about a decrease.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be only a moment or two, but I shall not be here to participate any further in the agriculture estimates because I must go to Toronto to-day. I want to help the minister if I can. For many years I too have listened to speeches that have been interpreted as creating conflifct between the east and the west. We do not want any conflict between the east and the west. We are dependent on one another; we cannot get along without one another. For my part I have been trying to redress the just complaints that the western people have made through these late years. They have been complaining because of conditions for which they were not responsible, conditions which we perhaps had not tried sufficiently to help them eliminate.

I am ready to support the minister in any programme he will bring in that will help the west. They are entitled to a programme which will relieve them from the menacing conditions under which they have had to operate. I have a keen recollection of going from Regina down through Weyburn to Estevan, and my heart would have broken, if it had not been strong, when I saw the frightful conditions of the farmers in that locality. They were up against calamity through no fault of their own. They put in their crops and they hoped for a return, but they did not get a return because the country was dried out. We gave them little assistance, and they came down here, and rightly so, to complain. I for one am finding no fault with the complaints they made.
The minister is too humble; he does not ask for enough. I will promise him that I will go right across the province of Ontario, to every town and city, and address boards of trade and chambers of commerce to ask for support for a programme that will bring the relief to the west that they are entitled to. Water should be brought to these dried-out areas. If the minister would suggest a programme to spend $5,000,000 for the building of a dam near Riverhurst to provide water required for all the land between the river and Regina-yes, and right down to Estevan-it would be a worth-while programme, a programme that the whole country should support.
There should be no conflict between the east and the west; there should be an endeavour on the part of the east to help the west get on its feet. A man cannot get on his feet in a dried-out area, but give bis land water and he will get on his feet. He will be able to produce cattle, grain, and everything else with which he can buy the things he needs. That would help your own city, Mr. Chairman, because mention has been made of agricultural implements, and they are made in the city of Brantford. The farmers would be able to buy such implements, but they cannot when they must live on dried-out land. They must have water.
I am going to appeal to the minister to bring in a programme for $100,000,000. That is not much; it is only the price of one battleship, and who worried over the sinking of a battleship during the last war? Nobody worried over that. We built more. Bring in a programme to provide irrigation for the dried-out areas in Alberta and Saskatchewan so that these good farmers-they are good farmers-so that these brave farmers-they

I want to compliment the minister upon the good work he has done, but he would have done much better if he had acted as I suggested and had not been so humble. He should have asked for what he requires. This land should be rehabilitated. The minister has done some fine work. Look at what has been done around Swift Current. This is evidence of what irrigation water will do. The farmers in that area are grateful. I do not want to take any more time, but I did want to say a word to encourage the minister to come out with a giant programme to give those western provinces a chance to Eve.

Mr. Chairman, it is just about two minutes to one o'clock and I understand we are to go on again at three. I did intend to make a statement this morning of the kind that was asked for by the hon. member for Souris, but I have been listening to speeches all morning which could more properly have been made on the different items. For example, the speech which has just been made with regard to irrigation i3 one which properly could have been made under prairie farm rehabilitation, for which we are going to vote money.
The programme my hon. friend has mentioned, that of $100,000,000, is the one I have been advocating, behind closed doors and everywhere else. I think if he reads my political speeches in the last campaign he will see that I advocated it every time 1 spoke.
I was too busy getting elected myself.

Everything that has
been mentioned in the debate so far, with the possible exception of the quota on the deliveries of wheat, was covered in the two speeches that I delivered on the address. There may be some justification for saying that jye have not taken sufficient time with agriculture during this session, and for that reason I wanted this debate to go on as freely as possible and as far as possible. However, we have been up three times with our estimates and I hesitate to start to make a general statement which will take half an hour or forty minutes and just repeat what I said on the address. I think if hon. members will read what I said then they will find the answers to the questions they have been asking, or to practically all of them. They will not find the answer to the question about the quota on wheat deliveries, because that
is not a matter with which I deal particularly; it is dealt with by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. But I am sure that in order to satisfy the curiosity of anyone who may wish to know, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not object if I say that it was not a matter of my choice, nor was it the choice of this government, except in the last analysis, that any limitation was put on the delivery of wheat for 1945. The policy which was stated by myself as Minister of Agriculture was that we should control as far as we possibly could the farmers' acreage in wheat from year to year. But the farm organization with which my hon. friend has been working for many years-as a result of that experience he has been able to demonstrate this morning a wide knowledge of the wheat question- put up a policy which we were following until compelled to discontinue. I stated definitely, both in the house and outside the house and in the discussions that took place, that from my experience in western Canada I was sure that no maximum quota placed on wheat could be maintained by any government or by any body trading in wheat if we had a crop failure in half of the west. That is what we have this year; therefore the fourteen-bushel quota had to be taken off. In other words I do not believe in a ceiling quota on wheat at all.
I want a floor, not a ceiling.

I do not believe in a ceiling quota. It is a ceiling quota when you say to a farmer, "You cannot deliver more than fourteen bushels to the acre." That is a ceiling, not a floor. I am not in favour of saying to any farmer in western Canada, after we have compelled him to accept ceiling prices throughout the war, that he is to be limited to any particular ceiling in delivering farm products after the war.
Neither am I.

I do not want it on wheat any more than I want it on anything else. But I do not want to be misunderstood on that point. Let me say that I think one of the best policies that ever has been introduced into western Canada was the placing of quotas on deliveries of wheat by saying at' the beginning of the season, "You can deliver only five bushels an acre off each farm." That permits the man twenty miles back from the railway to make his deliveries of wheat early in the season, and not have the elevators plugged full by the men who ' live within a mile or two miles of the elevators. Therefore, as far as the quota

deliveries are concerned, I hope they will never be discontinued, but I hope also that [DOT] at no time shall we say that we are going to stop the farmer at some particular point, definitely, in delivering his wheat year by year.
So do I.
But that was the policy we were asked to follow-280,000,000 bushejs to be delivered in a year or fourteen bushels to the acre of 20,000,000 acres.
Not less.

No, not more. That was all they guaranteed to take, and it was insisted that there should be no departure from that maximum. That was the policy we were asked to follow by the Saskatchewan wheat pool, by resolution, and in committees and everywhere else.
Does that apply to the deliverable quotas mentioned in the order in council?

No; I am trying to tell hon. members that so far as I am concerned in the government, it does not, and it never will. I hope there will not be very many coming from western Canada, who will be advocating a policy of that kind.
I sat here and listened to the discussion on the address. I let it go by because I hesitated at that time to say anything about what is being done in other countries. But we had an amendment to the address on the question of adopting practically the system which they have in the United States, of paying ninety per cent of parity. The system in the United States is based on the idea that no farmer who gets the benefits of that parity price will be able to deliver from more than a certain acreage or more than a certain quantity of his product. If any hon. member will take the trouble to go back and read the discussions on the floor prices he will find that fundamental in those discussions is the statement that we did not say to the farmer during war time, "You just produce a small amount" and then, "We are going to put a ceiling on it"; we said, "You produce all you can in order to feed the people of the world and then we will put a ceiling on it." And what I say is this: having said that during the war, when the war is over we ought to see that a floor is under it no matter how much you produce, and we ought to allow the farmer to deliver, at least for a period of time, at prices which will be such as to permit him to gain back any disadvantages he may have sustained
(Mr. Gardiner.]
because of the policy we followed during war time. That in a few words is my policy on this matter.
Is that going to be the minister's policy in future?
I cannot say that it will always be the policy of the government of Canada.
That is the important part.

You have sufficient confidence in me to say that if I decide that that is the proper agricultural policy for Canada, it will be carried out. So far there may have been some reason for saying that, but I am not at all sure that any policy I propose will always be carried out. But I am saying that the prices act under the legislation which passed this house in the session before the election did carry that idea in it, and it is on the statute books of this country, and if it is administered under myself as Minister of Agriculture in the Department of Agriculture as it is now, .it will be carried out in accordance with those principles, which are the principles hon. members have been advocating from all sides of the house throughout this whole debate. They are laid down there; they are in the legislation. Any floor prices which are set have to be set after full consideration has been taken of the relationship between the price of the farmer's product and the thing he has to buy, both in war time and in the period following the war, which is in general terms a parity relationship. We do not all agree what parity really is, and rather than saying "parity" it was put in general language which means that very thing.

I see there is a small increase in the amount available this year. At present it is not necessary to advertise agricultural products very much because there seems to be a ready market for them, but that is not going to obtain always. It has not in the past. Visiting Great Britain last fall I found that Australia and New Zealand are carrying on a much more aggressive advertising and sales policy over there than our department has carried on in the past. If we are to retain our market there, once competition asserts itself again, ,we shall have to carry on a more extensive publicity and advertising campaign in Great Britain.
That comes under item 28.
This has to do with publicity and extension.
It relates to the publications that we put out to inform people with regard to agriculture.
That is what I am talking about.
The hon. member is discussing advertising, and that comes under 28.

I will reserve my remarks, then, until we come to that item. Can the minister give us some details about these publications that are put out, and what has been done in this direction during the past ' year?

Perhaps it would be well for me to put on the record in a few sentences exactly what the division covers. The division assumes the responsibility of serving the whole department in maintaining contacts between technical and administrative officers of the various services and the farmers of Canada. This is accomplished through such well-recognized media as printed publications, press releases, radio broadcasts, educational displays at fairs and at exhibitions, lending libraries and lantern slides. The division operates a duplicating service for the whole department, maintains a mailing list, and undertakes the distribution of all market reports, educational literature and administrative information issued. The work of the division is conducted under the heading of administrative and editorial exhibits, press and publicity, and lantern slides service.

This is rather a small vote, although I regard it as one of the most important in all the estimates for agriculture. The publicity and extension division serves as'the connecting link between the farmers of Canada and the Department of Agriculture and its activities. There was a time in the history of Canadian agriculture when it was thought that anyone who was not very much good for anything else could become a successful farmer, but to-day agriculture is on an entirely different basis. It has become a more or less scientific occupation in which a man must be well trained if he hopes to succeed. As a matter of fact, farmers must have to-day a very wide knowledge covering a good many subjects if they wish to be successful. First of all they must know something about soil and soil composition, fertilizers and fertilizer values, grain and fodder crops, fruit and vegetable crops, growth and method of cultivation and so on. They must know something about the various insect pests that attack animals and plants. They must know something about plant diseases and how to combat them. They baust know something about live stock and what constitutes a good animal in any particular breed that they are trying to raise, as well as the conformation and type of animal and the best way in which they can raise good quality animals and produce the best commodities. Not only that, the farmers must know something about marketing and marketing requirements; the type of product needed on the markets, the qualities demanded, and the different types of animals that have to be raised. They must know a year ahead what will be the future demands of these markets.
, My point at the moment is that this publicity and extension division does not seem to be accomplishing all that it might do as a liaison between agriculture generally and the Department of Agriculture. There is not enough publicity. The farmers generally do not know enough about these publications and about what is being done to assist agriculture. Can the minister tell us how the general public is informed of these different bulletins that are put out from time to time? They ought to be of great value. They would convey to the farmers, if the farmers have the time and the opportunity to study them, what is being done in the department. There are a great many ways in which they could help the farmers to benefit by the findings of the department itself.

To answer both the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), I
Supply-Agriculture

might point out that this service has been carried on over a long period of years, ever since we have had a department, and it has naturally been growing from year to year. During the past year, sixty new and revised publications have been added to the number put out, and these include thirteen farmers' bulletins, one household bulletin, three technical bulletins, nine circulars, two acts, orders and regulations, fifteen special war-time production series, seventeen reports and miscellaneous publications. The number sent out was 1.229,182, merely on personal request. That will give an idea of the number of persons receiving these publications. It does not mean, of course, that this is the exact number of persons to whom publications were sent, because some persons might have three or four different requests, but it does show that there is close contact between the farmers throughout the country and those engaged in other businesses who are interested in farming and the department itself.
There are over 592,080 publications mailed in bulk for redistribution. They are sent out to secretaries of counties or municipalities in the west, or farm organizations. Any organization which is in close contact with the farmers and can make this distribution to people who do not personally send in for them, may get them. There are 1,218,894 copies of market reports mailed out on request. That would indicate that there is quite an interest in the marketing report. There are 9,025,863 copies of mimeographed', multigraphed and multilith press releases, news, market information, and so forth, sent out. Therefore it will be noted that there is a considerable distribution, to the public of farm pamphlets and farm information.

The information the minister has just given emphasizes the point I was trying to make. Undoubtedly those pamphlets are of great value to agriculture if they are distributed, and if the public know just what they are. The minister has said that some sixty new publications were brought out last year. Frankly I must say-and I keep in close touch with this thing-that I do not. know what those publications are. I may know a few of them. Some kind of advertising plan should be brought into effect which would let 'the farmers know what the publications are. I am pointing this out only because I think it is of real advantage to the farmers to have them. I think they can accomplish a great deal more if farm people generally have a better idea of what they are.

I do not know what
cooperation there is between the minister's department and the departments of agriculture in the provinces with regard to the distri-
bution of this information, but I would say that through their county and district representatives the departments of agriculture in the provinces are probably closer to their people than is the dominion Department of Agriculture. If the publications were made available to those representatives, and they were urged to see to it that the publications were distributed, it might tend' to get them into the hands of those who could use them to much greater advantage.

There is the utmost cooperation between the provincial departments and the federal department. First, there is a close check to make sure that provincial and federal publications do not overlap any more than is absolutely necessary; if t^e provinces get out a pamphlet on a certain subject we do not put out the same kind of pamphlet on the same subject. After that is done we see that the provinces are supplied with a reasonable number of whatever they find useful. We have a mailing list of all provinces which covers most of the secretary-treasurers of municipalities, farm organizations, and all people who would be naturally interested. Beyond that there are many people who attend a meeting, hear the publication referred to and write in for a copy of it. The long mailing list that I have here is a result of those communications.
The hon. member for Haldimand referred to something which I think I remember his having referred to five or six years ago. He will remember that on one occasion our mailing list was referred to, and it was pointed out that members of parliament >wh,o had passed away some years before were still getting the publications. As. a result of the criticisms made at that time we had the list largely revised, and we are not depending so much upon lists of that kind now as we are upon personal inquiries coming in. From then on we keep them on the list.

I do think some better plan should be devised to acquaint the public with 'the publications which are brought out from time to time. Farmers are getting into difficulties at all times. They have their difficulties in regard to production. For instance, science comes under the Department of Agriculture. Scientists are finding out new things all the time, things that are of great interest to the farmers, things that would save the farmer money if he knew about them. I suggest that some real plan should be devised to acquaint agriculture generally throughout Canada with the pamphlets that are being issued.

Has the minister considered a short intimation of the publications

Supply-Agriculture
or pamphlets being given to the weekly press of Canada? I do not remember the number of weekly newspapers there are in Canada, but I know in the riding of Yale, which is largely an agricultural riding, there are seven. If a short intimation was given to the weekly press of a new publication on such-and-such a subject it might bring it to the attention of the farmers who might not otherwise learn of it.

An announcement goes out every week to the weekly press. Anything new which turns -up is in that.
With further reference to what the hon. member for Haldimand has said, most of the new developments which take place are announced over the radio. It is felt that the farmer gets the announcement more readily in that way, and more farmers get it. It is thought to be more helpful to put it out in that way. But even after it is put out over the radio it is put in publication form and sent weekly to the press.

How many publications are issued regularly, monthly or weekly? What are their names? I receive one in my box entitled as I recall it, "Live Stock Review". How many others are there, and what are they called?
I think I gave, before the hon. member came in, the total numbers of the publications put out.
Are there certain ones which are issued every week and every month?

Yes. For example, there are 1,218,894 copies of market reports. They are mailed out on request. Those go out regularly. Then there are mimeographed copies. It would not be possible for me to give the list because it is a long one. Nine million of those go out, or have gone out during the last year. Then there are half a million publications mailed in bulk. I think those are the ones that the hon. member has in mind.
What are they called?
Those are publications on the production of dairy products, hogs, live stock generally, vegetables, fruits, and grains. The pamphlets that go out are all of that type.

Will the minister give a little more information as to how the facts are ascertained? For instance, I have heard drovers say that the reports which are published in regard to the prices on the live stock markets are not always correct. I suppose there is a regular way in which those prices are
ascertained from day to day and from week to week, but I have heard drovers, and on one occasion farmers as well, say that they are not correct at all.

The plan followed1 is
the one which has been followed for many years and which has, I think, proven very satisfactory. A report on the- prices comes out daily; I have it on my desk every morning. I think that is the one which the drovers have in mind when they say, that it is not exactly the prices they get on their market. I am speaking from memory and I may be a little out on the number of markets, but I understand they take nine of the main markets right across Canada, beginning with Vancouver on the west, and they take the average of those prices and give you both the high point and the low point in the market. You also get the average of the sales for the day. One drover may bring live stock on the market and get the top price, or he may bring it on at the low point, so he will say the average price reported is not the price he obtained. But if he goes to a little more trouble and- gets the list of actual sales such as is published in the Free Press-and no doubt in other papers as well, though I am more familiar with this one-he will see the prices at which the sales were made. Any drover or farmer can look up that list and see how many animals sold at such a price, but in a publication such as we put out it is impossible to give the price of every animal and every carload of animals. We just give the average price for the day or week over a considerable area.

Order. We are dealing now with specific items. The general discussion took place on the first item.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: I was just using that for purposes of comparison, and I wished to make the comparison as odious as possible. If it is a fact that agriculture is still the backbone of the country, then as a farmer and the representative of farmers I wish to pay a tribute to the' scientists who have done so muph for agriculture in this country. This matter has been broached two or three times already, but I should like to take a few minutes to bring the work of these men just a little more clearly to our attention, and! to explain how, as a farmer, I view the advantages we obtain from their efforts.
When I first came out here I settled in the north country. My farm is on the same parallel, Mr. Chairman, as Prince Albert ; and I found the atmosphere very frosty. To my regret I discovered that it was almost impossible to grow wheat because of this frost; and the first time I saw the scientists in action was when they assisted me to grow wheat in a district in which the growing season was not long enough. True, they did not affect the weather; but they got to work and introduced a new' variety of wheat with a shorter growing season. Very quickly there were developed early varieties. Men connected with agriculture will recognize these names:	Reward, Prelude, and Garnet. It
became possible not only to grow wheat in that district, but to grow it 150 miles farther north. That area was opened up as a wheat growing district, and all this was entirely due to the work of the agricultural scientists, and in particular the plant breeders' section.
After a number of years we ran into difficulties w'ith plant diseases. Hon. members - will recall the terrible losses suffered in western Canada through the disease known as rust. There w'as a time when it appeared that the wheat-growing industry out there was finished, because those waving fields of wheat w'hich were so aptly described last night, after attack by this disease became at the end of a few weeks entirely valueless. When an hon. member said that even at ten cents a bushel a farmer would still get a lot of money, he was not quite accurate, because in many 1 instances those wheat fields were never cut.
Because of the disease which had affected them it became necessary to burn the wheat in the fields.
There is an intensely interesting story behind the fight against rust. Plant pathologists got busy. They told us all about the disease-where it came from, how it worked, and what it did to the wheat plant. They described to us its life cycle, explained1 that it used the barberry bush as a host plant, and that until the disease had gone through that host plant it could not do any further damage. Obviously, then, the thing to do was to destroy all host plants, all barberry bushes. An attempt was made to do exactly that, but it was found impracticable. The result was that we returned to the scientists known as plant breeders. They told us that in the nurseries at the experimental farms and at universities varieties of wheat had' been developed that were immune and resistant to rust, and they proceeded to hybridize or cross these resistant varieties with some of our well known wheats. It is a long story; it took a long time, but eventually we got the varieties which we are now using in western Canada, and which are no longer being affected by rust. But we cannot stop there, because it was discovered there were a large number of varieties of rust. Just how many have been discovered up to this time I do not know. My last information was that there were twenty-three. We have wheat which is resistant to all twenty-three varieties. In any day in any year another variety may fee discovered. Since the rust diseases themselves can hybridize, we shall certainly have other varieties of rust which in their turn will attack our resistant plants, with great danger of our running into the same difficulty again, and with a loss of millions upon millions of dollars. So it becomes necessary to keep a staff of these men working constantly, men who will keep their eyes open and the nurseries occupied. Through their work we may be able to keep away from the diseases which attack our plants.
There are other diseases, such as smut and root rot. Within certain limits we have learned how to control smut, although one variety known as loose smut has not yet been controlled chemically. I understand there is a complicated hot water treatment through which grain may be passed, and which will destroy the loose smut, but this treatment is not very practicable. Certainly it cannot be carried out on farms, and the result is /that we are waiting for some further development at the hands of ou-r scientists, in the expecta-
Supply-Agriculture

tion that they will tell us how to control this loose smut, which incidentally is costing us many millions of dollars each year.
Root rot is coming into our fields in western areas, and each year is costing us large sums of money. There is no known absolute control, although scientists are still working on the subject. It is our hope that eventually they will find something to do away with root rot.
Turning for the moment from cereals, we know there are diseases of fruit, such as those mentioned a few days ago by one hon. member. In the aggregate these diseases cost a lot of money. We have diseases of vegetables, including potatoes. In fact, a disease of that kind may attack even the 500 bushels clubs of the hon. member for Fort William. He may find disease among his spuds, in which event he would not have 500 bushels, and probably not even five. I hope the disease will not come near him, but of course there is a possibility that it may. Again our scientists are at work trying to meet the disease. So it goes, all down the line, in live stock as well as in plant life.
One of the. points I wished to make is one which has already been 'made, that our scientists are not receiving much encouragement to stay on their jobs. Their salaries are distressingly low-entirely too low. As a farmer and one who really appreciates what these men are doing and have done, I would plead that their rates of salary be made sufficient to induce them to stay in the country. May I read briefly on this point from the "Agricultural Institute Review" of September, 1945:
First, consider one individual who, in addition to two summers' work has served the division of botany continuously for ten years, after obtaining a Ph.D. degree. It was three years before this person obtained .any classified position, and, even then, was classified as an agricultural assistant, grade II, at a salary of $1,800 a year.
Just $1,800 a year.
Three years later this was reclassified to an agricultural scientist, grade I, with a salary range of $1,800 to $2,160 a year, and there, four years later and at the end of ten years' service it still stands.
That is nut very much money. Other cases are set out which I shall not detail. One to which I would refer, however, is described as follows:
One has been with this laboratory 17 years. During the summers of 1928. 1929 and 1930 he served at a salary rate of $1,320 per year. Then came the lean years and it was not until six years later he once again reached the $1,325 point, having served .at as low a salary as $1,118 in -the meantime. Not until 1938 did he reach $1,800, and since 1940 he has been at the maxi-

mum of his present class at $2,160. Think of that-after 17 years of service! Even when you add to this the $78.12 cost of living bonus which he receives

And here is the point:
-he is getting less than $200 more per year, than is the greenhouse attendant at the same laboratory.
I should like also to read a short paragraph from the thirty-fifth annual report of the Civil Service Commission of Canada, as follows:
The commission regrets that action has not been taken to restore annual increases to those permanent employees who are in receipt of salaries in excess of $3,000 -per annum. Many of these employees have been denied not only annual increases but also, for several years, the right of reclassification, while temporary employees in units which are recognized by the treasury board as "war units'' have been accorded the right of reclassification at all salary levels. Such differentiation results in a dissatisfied service and affects efficiency, and it is the opinion of the commission that the restoration of annual increases to all permanent employees is in the interests of good administration and the efficiency of the service.
The next report for -the year 1944 states:
There is a serious need for immediate adjustment in the compensation for' the professional, scientific and technical services, and the _ commission, after a comprehensive study, is of opinion that action should be taken -at once to improve the situation. Assurance of a reasonable salary attainable within a few years is necessary to retain those remaining in these services, and to attract new personnel for the planning and carrying out of the work of the post-war period. The loses that have been incurred in professional, scientific and technical ranks continue to result in expensive administration and the development of particularly critical situations in -those fields where the service is in direct competition with the commercial and industrial employer.
In the last five or six years some sixty-one scientific men have left the civil service to take better jobs. I had their classifications and salaries in the service and an estimate of what they were receiving in -the positions they took, but I seem to have mislaid it for the time being, so I will just suifimarize. When I had the opportunity of speaking before I made the statement that I -believed after the war the only countries able to stay in business would be those able to produce most economically. The control of disease, particularly plant disease and those affecting cereals, the control of insect pests, the improvement of cultural methods and soil improvement, all cut d-own production costs. Those things are in the hands of our scientists. I-t is quite conceivable that this country might have to quit growing wheat for export if some other country got- just a little ahead of us in scientific research and .'were able to produce better
