wheat and more of it. That is all scientific work. It is much to be hoped that when these things are discovered they will be discovered by the scientists in our own country. I ask the minister to give special consideration to the encouragement of the scientific men who at the present time are engaged in agricultural w<?rk.

I would point out that the hon. member stayed quite closely with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, at the beginning and end of wh^t he said. There are some hon. members who may not be fully acquainted with the procedure. The procedure has been to discuss in a general -way all that is under items from 5 to 11 under the first item which covers science service administration. Then we go on to deal with matters having to do with botany and plant pathology, for example, or with animal and poultry pathology under the items so-called. Much of what the hon. member said in the middle of his remarks would come under item 8. Perhaps we could have the general discussion with regard to all these matters on the first item of the group, and then take up the other items such as botany and plant pathology, animal' and poultry pathology, and so on. The salaries paid and the treatment given to men who are doing this work is a proper matter to be dealt with under this item, and I should like to make a few remarks in that connection.
It is admitted, I think by all members of the government and everyone concerned that the civil service of Canada was not well paid in many of its branches prior to the war. During the period of the war there was no opportunity to make a change in the actual payments or in the basis of payment. Now that the war is over certain adjustments are being made.
One of the reasons why we were in a difficult position, particularly in agriculture, prior to the war was that our expenditures down to about 1930, owing largely to conditions which existed in the country during the immediate preceding period, had gone up to something in the neighbourhood of ten or eleven millions for ordinary expenditure^. During the five years immediately following that they dropped back to about eight millions a year, which was the figure at the beginning of 1936 when I took over the department. Then I think they went up again to about eleven millions just prior to the war. During the war they dropped back again to a figure close to that at which they started.
Here are the exact figures. The appropriation for 1938 was $9,383,000; for 1939,
$10,000,000 and for 1940, $13,000,000. We got up to $13,000,000 at that time, but the expenditures were actually $11,816,000. Then we dropped back in 1941, under war conditions, to about $8,600,000. We continued at that figure down to 1943, and then we went up a little in 1944. This year, according to the figures in the estimates, we are asking for a vote of $10,256,250.
I would call attention to the fact that the figure stated by the last speaker at the beginning of his remarks is hardly a fair indication of the difference between the vote this year and the vote last year. The vote last year for the same purposes was $10,569,000, so there is a difference of $313,000. The total figure down below includes specials, and if you will note above you will see that the reduction has almost entirely to do with the wheat acreage reduction. As is known, we were paying out enormous sums of money a few years ago to obtain wheat acreage reductions. The difference there is the difference between $600,000 and $4,265,000. Almost the entire drop is due to the fact that we are not now paying wheat acreage reductions, most of the final payments having been made last year. There is a sum of $600,000 provided to clean up the last payments in 1945. The proper comparison should be between $10,500,000 and $10,256,000. Although it may be a little out of order, in view of the figure given by the hon. member at the beginning of his remarks I thought I should like to give the proper comparison.
Something has been said about the payments for science services. I would remind hon. members that on April 1 of this year the treasury board made a decision to the effect that those, for whom gross injustice had been created through the range of their salaries were to be given consideration on request of the various departments. The Department of Agriculture immediately took advantage of that suggestion, and we have had a very con- * siderable change made in salaries for persons such as those who have been referred to. For example,, the first person mentioned by the hon. member for North Battteford was, as he said, in the salary range $1,800 to $2,160, the last range which, I think, the hon. member quoted. He was on April 1 obtaining the maximum of that range, namely $2,160. Under the new salary range he is in the class from $2,820 to $3,180. In other words, he has an immediate increase of $660 per year and an ultimate increase of $1,020.

That is effective now, is it?

It is effective so far as he is concerned from April 1. I could go down through the list. There is quite a list here, and all these men are dealt with in that proportion. '
Does that take into account the cost of living bonus he was getting before? As I understand, he is not getting that today.
Well, there is no bonus in respect of salaries over $3,000. Of course immediately this man goes over $3,000 he will not have any bonus.
But is he going to get the bonus until that time?
This is net salary.
The $2,160 which he got before was not a net salary at that time; in addition he got the cost of living bonus.

Yes, he got a cost of living bonus during part of the war period, from the time cost of living bonuses were put on, and they are still on. He will get the cost of living bonus until he is entitled to a salary of $3,000. Probably the bonus will not be on for very long; however, that is another matter.
Under the division of botany, which has been referred to, there have been thirty-six reclassifications, and there are another twenty-six to be made. I state this in order to indicate that what has been suggested is at present being done.
There is one matter to which I should like to refer for a few moments because of the general nature of the discussion which is going on in connection with these matters. There seems to be a tendency to make comparisons. Some of us in this house have university degrees, and we know what the value of a university degree is. Others have not university degrees; and I doubt very much if there are many hon. members who, having listened to the various hon. members address themselves to the house, can determine just which have university degrees and which have not. Again, people take university degrees for different- reasons. Some take them in order to get a general education and be able to apply that education to any activity in life; others take them for the purpose of getting employment of a kind which does not require them to do manual labour. But I have been associated with government since 1914, and during the greater part of that time have had something to do with hiring civil servants, and I want to say that personally, and in spite of the fact that I have a university degree, I

resent very much seeing, in advertisements which come out from time to time for certain appointments, the intimation that a man must have a university degree in order to apply. I am inclined to think that all too often that qualification is used to eliminate a lot of people from civil service employment, and it is a very simple way of eliminating numbers of people who have good experience and good qualifications. I am not one of those who believe that you can simply say that, a man must have a university degree, or that he should be paid on a certain basis simply because he has a university degree. As a .matter of fact many of those degrees do not have a very close association with what a man is doing.
Eor example, I was listening to a discussion of this question a day or two ago, and one of the arguments put forward wras that a certain man was a plumber, another man had a university degree. I said then, and I am going to say now, that I did mot know which of them put in the most time learning the job he is doing, and I am not prepared to say that the job of the plumber is not just as important, as the jobs of some others. We would find great difficulty in carrying on some of the scientific researches that are spoken of if we did not have any plumbers, no matter how many research men we had. That may be true in many other directions. So I say that sometimes we may over-emphasize the matter of paying one particular group of people at a high rate because of certain academic qualifications they have. I believe that in a democratic country, or indeed in any country, the most important people are the people who work with their hands. They are the people who produce the food and the mineral wealth, and who turn out the manufactured products. They are the most essential. Take these men away from our operations, and it will not make very much difference how many scientists you have. Somebody has to get right down to doing the work. I think I would be safe in saying that at least seventy-five per cent-the proportion is probably low-of the pe9ple of this or any other country which has to be developed as Canada must be developed if we are to maintain the population we are capable of maintaining, must get right down to working with their hands. So I am in agreement with those who have been urging all the way through these estimates that the man who works with his hands-as farmers do-is entitled to just as good pay as anybody else. I am not particularly moved by the argument that a man is entitled to special consideration simply because he has qualifications which he got

largely through the help of the state-for most of our institutions which make it possible for men to get that type of education are sustained from the tax rolls of the people of the country. Because he has had the opportunity of taking advantage of the facilities provided by those educational institutions he is where he is to-day. There are other men who are just as essential, and I think we must see to it that they get their proper return.
I admit all that has been said on behalf of the scientists. I think they are not paid as much as they should be paid. I want them to be paid more, and I am going to see to it that scientists in the Department of Agriculture are treated at least as well as those in any other department of government.
There is a question on the order paper-I am sorry the answer was not down before this discussion took place, because I am sure the hon. member who asked it wanted the answer for the purpose of using the information here -as to how many men in the Department of Agriculture have certain degrees. Well, it is not nearly _ so important to know that as to know how many of those men have-
Brains.

Well, I would not put it that way; I think the fact that they are working in the agriculture department indicates that. But I would say it is important to know' if the man who has a degree is working in a job in which that degree is of any use to him. I can think of many jobs in the department where the possession of a degree does not necessarily give a man an advantage over one who has had five years' experience doing the work somewhere. On that basis I would say this. I hope that everyone in the department will be properly paid, but coming back to the first point I made, namely that our estimates were up to eleven millions and then went down to eight and then back to eleven and down to eight again, being now over ten millions, I venture to say that during the whole of that period we did not fire many because we had too many. If hon. members will look at the statistics they have been getting they will find that our staffs have been increasing year by year until they are higher to-day than at the time we were spending eleven millions or when we had an estimate of thirteen millions. We did not fire men when it was impossible for them to get jobs in other places; we kept them on. The fact that we had cut our estimates meant that we were paying as much in salaries but could not afford to give them as much money with which to do the job they were doing, and
therefore we could not use their services to the same extent that we had been doing earlier.
Some credit has to be given to governments generally for anting somewhat differently from industry in many instances. We speak of high salaries in industry, or of high wages, but w'e all know what the first thing is that has been done in the past, though I hope it will not be the first thing to be done in the future, when times get tough. The first thing that has been done in the past under those circumstances has been to turn out on the street the fellow who is not needed and allow the state to look after him.
Something was said at the beginning of the discussion about men coming back to the ' farms. The fact is that farmers looked after their own unemployed during the depression period. They kept their sons and daughters at home. There was not all the work to be done that they could have done on the farm. They may have worked hard but they could have been done without as was shown during war time, and one of the reasons why four hundred thousand men and women will not go back to farms lies in a fact, which explains many of these things, that I learned while the discussion was on. There was in New Brunswick a family who had lived in that province .four generations. First there were two people who came and settled on a one hundred acre farm, and now, four generations later, there are 610 people descended from those two. Those who argue that everyone who leaves the farm ought to go back should consider this fact. I should like to know how they would keep 610 people on that farm. That is the process that has been going on from one generation to another. We are living on family-sized farms. Only two people can live on that farm in the next generation, one of the sons of the farmer and one of. his neighbour's daughters. They will raise their family and in the next generation only two can stay on the farm, and so on. As long as the country is divided into family-size farms it is not going to be,possible to send all of each generation back to the farm, whether they have been at war or wherever they may have been. We have to keep that in mind.
We must remember that if we are going to make agriculture successful in the west, or in any other part of the country, we must make use of the scientists and others to find new uses for farm products, to convert them into the things that people need elsewhere; and more than anything else we must persuade the people of eastern Canada and the people of Britain that we want some of the eastern
Supply-Agriculture

industry in the west. I do not know of any better place for the development of industry in Canada than around the foothills of the Rocky mountains and in the country north of Winnipeg where there is power. I do not know of anything better for the development of our water resources, which have been spoken of. So that we need these scientists, both in the department and outside, to help us to develop these things, and I am going to fight to get as high salaries as we can for them, taking into consideration the fact that every other minister is fighting in the same way in his own department.

I was glad to hear the minister's statement. As I have said on several other occasions, I believe that he and his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce are putting up a brave fight for the farmers of Canada-not for the farmers of western Canada but for those of the country as a whole-and I hope they will be successful in pulling the wool from the eyes of their colleagues in the cabinet. We farmers must stick together. I have no degree, but I think that even without a degree a little common- horse sense will take one pretty far, and without horse sense, even if you have a degree, you will not get very far.
It is realized now, as it has been for a long time, even though some people will not admit it, that -the best potential market industry has in the west is the farming population. I have upstairs a letter which I intended to bring down, written to the Western Producer not long ago by a Saskatchewan farmer, showing all the items that have been manufactured in different parts of Canada, mainly in central Canada, and in use on the farms of the west. It goes to show that in practically everything the farmer uses, from the time that the alarm clock rings in the morning to wake him until he has finished separating the milk at night with the Renfrew or some other machine, he is using Ontario-made goods. The -minister is on -the right track, and I hope he will continue along that line and put up the fight he has made in the past.
I was glad- to hear the remarks of the hon. member for North Battleford with regard) to scientists. Scientists are -needed in agriculture as much as if not -more than in any other industry, for various reasons, many of -which the hon. gentleman outlined. I might say that the hon. member -was speaking what he honestly and truly 'believes, -because his son is qualified to act as district agriculturist for the Alberta government in my constituency, and he is doing a good job too. I am satisfied that he was speaking his mind sincerely. There is one variety of wheat which he left out, how-

ever, when he was discussing cereals. It was developed not very far from Ottawa by Ontario -people. One of the Manitoba members described that wheat to me some time ago. He said that it had grown normally and- after fifty or sixty years had reached maturity. Those who were experimenting -with it took it part of the time as a joke-to-day most of us regard it in the same light-and when it came to maturity these people found that-there was nothing in it except chaff. The name of that wheat is Renfrew North.

I too welcomed the first part of the minister's statement regarding the classification of salaries of scientific personnel in his department. But I think it was most unfortunate that the -minister proceeded to drive a wedge 'between those who work with their hands and those who are scientific workers in- his department. He admitted what many people feared1 during the thirties when he took the point of view that because farm prices were at such very low levels the salaries of scientific workers in the Department of Agriculture should be kept down. If every department of government had carried that out, there would not be any grounds for complaint. But an examination of the Department of Justice or the Department of Finance or any -other department would indicate that judges, for example, were not expected to be kept on an income that would correspond with the income that was going to farmers who were selling eggs at three or four cents a dozen and butter at ten cents a pound. This committee might expect the Minister of Agriculture to insist that personnel in his department should receive remuneration at least comparable with those in other departments of government, and I am sure that has not been the case.
To emphasize the point that I think should be made regarding the contribution which has been made to our life in Canada by the scientific workers, I shall mention two or three names that I picked out at random when the estimates were before the committee a year ago. I asked the minister then how long those particular employees had been with the government. The minister did not have the information, but said offhand, eight or ten years. Here is the name of W. C. Broadfoot. Doctor Broad'foot was one of my - classmates at university. He was one of the best hockey players and an excellent rugby player. I think he might have gone into professional athletics and made a very good living, but he was interested in scientific problems. He went to the university of Minnesota, as I recall it, and secured a doctor's degree there. If I remember correctly

he graduated in 1923, twenty-two years ago. So far as I know he has devoted his full time during those years to scientific problems. According to the public accounts he is now getting S2.880, which, in my opinion, is entirely inadequate when one considers the training - he had' before entering the department and the contribution he has made since.
Here is R. C. Russell in the same salary classification. Mr. Russell was one of my own instructors when I was at university. I think it is twenty-three or twenty-four years since he was doing post-graduate work; but he was an excellent instructor and taught the members of our class the history of rust. So far as I know he has been working for many years on problems associated with rust; and when hon. members consider what Thatcher wheat or any of the other rust-resistant wheats have meant in dollars and cents to the people of this country, to keep a university graduate with all the experience he has had on a salary of $2,880 compared with some of the salaries we pay to personnel in War Assets Corporation or Munitions and Supply or the wartime prices and trade board is demoralizing to say the least to the highly trained personnel who are doing this kind of work.
I think it would have been much better if the minister had left unsaid the last part of1 his speech, and had concluded by merely saying that so far as he was concerned university graduates in his department are going to have compensation according to their ability, commensurate with the compensation being paid to scientific workers in other parts of government. Could the minister indicate whether these two men I have mentioned in botany and plant pathology, W. C. Broad-foot and R. C. Russell, have been entitled to any increase in salary in the reclassification mentioned?

Both of the men who have been mentioned have not yet been classified, but they are in the next group to be classified. The men are being taken in groups through the department and a certain group dealt With at one time and a certain group at another, as is necessary in dealing witli that kind of thing. These two men are under consideration at the present time and will have their salaries adjusted in line with what I stated in regard to the others.
Now, as to the driving of wedges, I do not know of any better wedge-driver with whom I have come in contact since I have been in public life than the member for Mackenzie. Instead of driving wedges I was simply saying that all our people have to be dealt with on the same level in accordance with the work
they are doing. There is no wedge-driving in that. The wedge-driving would be if you got one group out of line with another; and I am suggesting that it is wedge-driving when you take a man who has a university degree and compare him with a man who is a competent plumber or something else, and say merely because the one man has a university degree and the other is a plumber that the man with the university degree should get more. That is the real wedge-driving that I have heard going on for some considerable time.
I did not say anything about a plumber.

No, but you said I was driving wedges. I can tell you that you drove more wedges in the few minutes that you were on your feet than I did in the time I was speaking. The situation is that we need all classes of men in a department, and any wedges which my hon. friend attempts to drive by misstating what I said, by saying that back in some other period, we kept salaries down is contrary to the facts. We did not do any such thing. From the time we came into office in 1935 we raised the salaries.
And kept men temporary for years.

There have been men on the temporary staff here because of regulations which existed. A man is sometimes called a temporary for twenty years. The fact that he is a temporary does not mean that his pay is less; it means that he is not on the list of those who will get superannuated until he goes on to the permanent staff.
Mr. NICHOLSON; That is keeping wages down.
That is a regulation which has been here for a long time. Only a certain percentage of those in each group are raised up to the-
The minister had a very large percentage of the total personnel.
Not very many in our department.
There were a few years ago.

We have temporaries, of course, who are employed during the summer months at the experimental farms. They are temporaries because of the fact that they work only during part of the year, and their

wages are regulated partly by what farmers are able to pay in those districts. Those men are doing farm work.
The minister had temporaries in his own office.
In our department as there are temporaries in every department. Ours is not any different from any other.
The minister's is the worst.

Ours is not the worst. I should like my hon. friend to tell us when we raised the wages of judges. Simply to take two or three departments, name them, and say that one department does this and another department does that, does not help. The civil service commission controls the payments in all departments. Their chief job is to see that the payments for similar work in one department is exactly the same as it is in another. That is not my job at all; that is the job of the civil service commission. They take the men who are scientists in our department and men who are scientists in other departments; they classify them, and they see that men in one classification in my department are paid exactly the same as men in the same classification in another department. If they make a mistake on that, we ask them for a reclassification, and we keep battling away until we get ours on the same standard as they are in any other department. That is the plan followed. Simply to get up and say that in one department they are doing this and in another department they are doing that is only saying that the civil service commission, which was set up by this house, not by any department, is not doing its job as it was intended it should do it, and I am not prepared to say that that is the case. I am prepared to say that it has a big job to . do, and that it may reclassify the employees of the agriculture department now and may not reclassify the employees of the other departments until later. As a matter of fact that is the case. I think I can say that the Department of Agriculture is farther along the way-I am assured that that is true-in the reclassification upwards of salaries than any other department of government as a result of the ruling made on April 1. No longer ago than the day before yesterday I sat in with the representatives of the civil service who are interested in this particular point and discussed with them everything that has been discussed here this afternoon. Most of the illustrations that have been given today were mentioned then, and time after time I was told that the Department of

Agriculture was further advanced than any other department in this matter of reclassification. By that I do not mean anything detrimental to the other departments. The department which applies is selected and gone through with.
Agriculture was the worst, was it?

It is the best at the moment, and it was never the worst. It has been well toward the top all the way through. So wdien my hon. friend gets up and follows his old custom of mentioning some particular hardship somebody is suffering, and bases an argument on that, I am afraid he will have to pick on some other department than agriculture.

What is the department

No, I believe we are
keeping control of it.
I thought some $300,000 or $400,000 had been given to another department to deal with this problem.
I think I said at an earlier stage that money was voted to the Department of Reconstruction, but it does not necessarily follow that the money will be spent by that department.
You handle that?

We make application to them for the money when required, and we handle it; it is just a matter of getting the-money from them.
The present spruce budworm' outbreak extends from the eastern boundary of Manitoba to the St. Maurice valley in the province of Quebec. An area of approximately 260,000 square miles is involved. The. same outbreak has spread also during the last year from Canada into the United States, where it covers some 12,000 square miles in the state of New York and a considerable area in the state of Vermont. To all appearances, this outbreak is more than likely to spread into the maritime provinces within the next four or five years. The areas of heaviest infestation in eastern Canada are in the vicinity of lake Nipigon, the Mississagi district, Algonquin Park and an area immediately north of this near lake Abitibi, lake Temiskaming and the Coulonge river watershed. Over some 25,000 square miles practically all the balsam and between 50 and 60 per cent of the white spruce has been completely destroyed. An additional
Supply-Agriculture

area of 45,000 square miles is in immediate danger of total destruction. Approximately 180,000 square miles are now lightly infested.
Intensive studies of the outbreak are in progress in all the affected regions. New developments in connection with spread of the outbreak are being closely followed through the dominion forest insect survey. Studies in control methods have been undertaken by the dominion government and the provincial governments. Three distinct experiments in chemical control by the distribution of D.D.T. from aeroplanes were attempted in 1945. Preliminary tests of the effectiveness of various dosages were made in the early spring in Algonquin park on six 10-acre plots. More elaborate experiments of the same nature, covering an area of approximately 2,000 acres in the Kabonga region of the province of Quebec, have yielded considerable information with regard to the effectiveness of aeroplane spraying. The largest undertaking of this kind consisted in the spraying of some 100,000 acres in the Nipigon district.

What cooperation has taken place between the federal and the provincial departments? Where does the Department of Reconstruction enter the picture? This is a serious matter in several large areas, and great acreages of forests might be completely lost.

On September 14, 1945, a coordinating organization known as the forest insect control board was established by order in council under the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. It will be the duty of the board to take all possible steps, both separately and in cooperation with the provinces and forest industry, to control forest insect outbreaks, particularly the spruce bud-worm. I understand that the very best of cooperation is being established between the department here and the provincial departments in carrying this out.
What effect has D.D.T. had on persons and birds in that district?
I understand that there are no serious effects on either human beings or birds.

I believe this item deals with a most important branch of the Department of Agriculture, one which has been and is doing good work throughout 'Canada. I should, however, like to take a moment or two to make some suggestions respecting experimental farms.
Much has been done by different boards set up to increase production throughout Canada to meet contracts with Great Britain. We are sending large quantities of bacon, beef, cheese, eggs and seeds to the people of Great Britain and Europe, but I am afraid that not enough has been done to see that we retain those markets. The minister may not agree with me in this. I know he has a contract with Great Britain for certain lines of farm products, up to the end of 1946. However, even at this time other countries in Europe from which Great Britain received her supplies in other days are now entering the British market.
I would speak particularly for a moment or two upon our bacon market over there. All hon. members will agree that our shipments of bacon overseas during the war have brought great benefit to the Canadian people in general and our farmers in particular. There are two main things that must be looked after if we are not going to lose our market in England for bacon as we did after the last war. The first., of course, is maintenance of the quality of our bacon. Then we must keep up the continuity of supply. This has been mentioned so often that it is not necessary for me to elaborate on it. If we are to maintain our market we must see that those two things are carried into effect.
I doubt if the reputation of Canadian bacon has been increased very much during the past four or five years. We are sending over to England some sixteen different grades of bacon, and we have been doing this for some time. What we have sent has not always been of the best and it has not always gone over in continuous supply. Denmark was a large producer of bacon and sent considerable quantities to Great Britain in days gone by, and that country is again entering the market. In Denmark they have a system that is far in advance of ours in producing good quality bacon. There is a good deal of government supervision and control over the production of hogs and bacon, particularly bacon that is to go to England. The control over production is rigid; there is control over marketing and over quality; there is control as to what proportion of fat and lean there shall be; there is control over the size of the carcass and the shape of the sides are controlled. As I said before, I do not believe-the reputation of our bacon in England has increased much during the war years.
Moreover. I do not believe the quality of our hogs has improved during the war years. Every select hog produced in this country receives a bonus of $4, and if I am correctly informed the production of select hogs has increased only from thirty-three tp thirty-seven per cent during the war. That is not a Very large increase considering the bonus which is paid. I believe hog producers should take a leaf out of the book of the dairy industry! In the dairy industry they use good sires and dams, and I believe this is done largely in the production of hogs. But in spite of all that has been done, we find that while there may be hogs of good conformation, there are other hogs with some malformation which makes it impossible for them to be brought to maturity. A hog may have a rupture or other malformation.
Then the dairy industry has what is known as a record of performance. An animal may be a good type and of good conformation, but it may not be a good producer. Something should be done to see that we produce hogs of good type and of good conformation which are also good producers. We see in the papers many advertisements about the use of feed. Some people say that you can produce a pound of pork with six pounds of grain; others say you need only five pounds, and some get as low as three and a half pounds. We should have hogs which are not only of good conformation and good type but which make rapid gains in growth. Producers throughout the country are doing a great deal to improve our hogs in every way, but they cannot do everything. They are not always wealthy men, and they cannot afford to weed out hogs which are not the best type or which may have some defect or malformation.
I believe the time has come when our experimental services should set up some kinds of stations to increase these particular qualities in our hogs. At the time of the Winnipeg convention there was inserted in the agricultural platform of the party to which I belong a clause reading as follows:
To set up a swine study superstation with sufficient facilities and personnel for an exhaustive study of measures for the improvement of the Canadian bacon hog and of means to retain after the war our present quota of bacon exports.
That is something which should be done by the experimental farms branch. It will have to be done by some government agency because private interests cannot afford to do

it. I make that proposition to the minister and to the government because I believe it is a sound one. I believe it would be of real assistance to the hog industry in the Dominion of Canada.
I should like to make another suggestion. This may not meet with the approval of the committee, but I think it is worth while. In Denmark they have breeding stations; the farmer does not raise his own little pigs; they are raised in breeding stations under strict government supervision and control. That may seem visionary at the present time and it mayr be that the farmers of Canada' would prefer to breed their own little pigs, but I would point out that twenty-five years ago there were very few chick hatcheries in the Dominion of Canada. To-day there are very few chicks raised in any other way, because the people producing poultry and eggs buy their chicks from the chick hatcheries which are under inspection and supervision. I believe the time has come at least to make an experiment in that direction.
I believe little pigs could be raised to better advantage in breeding stations which would be under supervision and control and where the conditions would be better for the breeding and selection of pigs. It is said that from twenty-five to thirty per cent of our little pigs perish before they grow up, before they are of any great age. That sort of thing *does not occur any more in the chick hatcheries. The mortality rate of small chicks in chick hatcheries is very small and I think the same results could be obtained if we had breeding stations for hogs. The small pigs would get better care and they would be less liable to disease; they would get a better diet and, if the stations were properly equipped and the personnel properly qualified, it would go a long way to producing a more uniform type of hog throughout the Dominion of Canada. #
There is another reason which I think is just as important. At certain periods of the .year we have large runs of hogs coming on to the market, so much so that it is almost impossible for the abattoirs to handle them. At other seasons of the year there are only small runs coming on to the market and the abattoirs cannot keep busy. If breeding stations were established throughout the *country I believe it would tend to keep a uniform supply of hogs coming on to the market at all seasons of the year. I suggest that the packers themselves would be very well advised to experiment with this thing to see how it would work out, because after all the packers are just as much interested as

the farmers are. We need the packers to process our animals; at the same time the packers need the farmers to raise the animals; and if the packers could, by means of an experimental breeding station, demonstrate that they could raise more and better hogs, and that they could distribute those hogs over the year, it would be a great advantage to the packers as well as to the farmers. I leave these suggestions with the minister because I believe they are worth considering.

Not Calgary.

The hon. member had better examine his maps. I have had to draw a line around that area for the purposes of the Prairie Farms Rehabilitation Act. The reason there is P J'Jt.A. work out there is that it is in the Palliser triangle. If you draw a line from Morden in Manitoba, straight west to Lloydminster; then another line straight from Lloydminster bo the foothills west of Calgary, and then go to the boundary line you have the Palliser triangle inside of that to the south. There are a million people living there, and with all due respect to those who think they should not have been put there I should like to know just where you could put a million people if you took them out of that area. I should like to know where else you could plump them down and have them do any better than they are doing at present if you took them out of that area.
Some people have said they have moved back from the west, and others have said they have moved west. That is because of what we like and do not like in the way of climate and in the way of making our living. Out there we have illustration stations largely because of what was said by one hon. member a few minutes ago, that there was a time when they could not grow wheat in the dis-

Supply-Agricul ture
trict in which he lives; but they grow wheat there now because of the activities of some of these people who have been carrying on experiments. In the district in which I live it is not many years ago that they could not grow wheat, though I live just north of the Qu'Appelle valley. They had to grow oats and raise live stock; but to-day they grow wheat almost exclusively. Those conditions were changed not because the weather changed or because the soil changed, but because somebody carried on experiments and discovered wheat that could be produced in a short season. Not only did they carry on experiments; some breeding was done which made it possible to get wheat-which could be used in those areas. The tests are made in regard to that breeding by taking the wheat from the experimental farm to the illustration stations and trying it under those soil conditions. If it will produce in a certain length of time, or if it is free of rust attacks during certain seasons, then we continue to grow that type of wheat there. That is the real reason why the stations, are located at different points all over western Canada, not only in Saskatchewan but throughout Manitoba and Alberta. More of them are in Saskatchewan than in any other province because, as some hon. members opposite have been trying to demonstrate for some days, we think we have more problems than the other provinces.

Before this item passes, I should like to come back to Ontario for a little while. Would the minister tell us something about the number of illustration stations in Ontario? I am thinking particularly of a newly projected station just west of the town of Trenton, along lake Ontario. I should like to know what kind of work it is going to do, what the staff will be, and so on.

It is really a small experimental farm that has been established at Trenton. The staff will not be large; that is the permanent staff, but we will send men there from the central experimental farm here to do a considerable portion of the work. A skeleton staff will be there all the time operating that farm.
What is the nature of the work to be carried out there? Is it to be purely in connection with the apple growing industry, or is it to render a general service?

The work is experimenting in the best methods of building and maintaining orchards, treating apple and other fruit trees with spray, and the best methods of producing vegetables in that dis-47696-1661
trict. I was at that farm within the last three months, and was pleased to see the development that has taken place.
We are grateful to see some move made in regard to growing apples.

While we are on this item I should like to put in a word for the dominion experimental substation at Delhi. Mr. Stinson, who is in charge there, is doing a very good job in experimental work in connection with tobacco. I know during the war he was handicapped by lack of help; now he would like to make some extensions'-to his plant, so that I just want to draw this-matter to the attention of the department in the hope that he will be given every consideration.

I am pleased to have' that statement with regard to the Delhi farm.. I understand that the two men who were' employed there as assistants before the war and who have been overseas are returning to the farm, so that we hope it will operate with greater efficiency in future than has.been possible during the war.
Will the minister state whether any experimental or research work along forestry lines is being carried on under the experimental farms branch?

Yes; we have the forestry nursery stations at Indian- Head and Saskatoon, with which I am sure the leader of the opposition is quite familiar. These stations supply forestry plants for all four provinces.
Formerly they were under another department, were they not?
I understand that at one time they were under the Department of the Interior, but that was before my time.

I am asking this question because, as I remember the remarks of the Minister of Reconstruction the other day on another matter, he indicated that certain research work along forestry lines was being undertaken by that department. This may not be a matter I should discuss now; I am not particularly anxious to do so, but I want to know when it might be discussed. I am wondering, though, since forestiy work is already being done in one or two other places, why research work in forestry should be placed under still another department. I do not ask that much time be taken on the point now, but perhaps the minister could say a word about it.
Supply-Agriculture

I understand that the work, really is to be done under the Department of Mines and Resources, which is the continuation of the old interior department. That work is in connection with natural forests. The work we are doing at the two forestry farms is reproducing trees which will grow well in different localities, and distributing those trees, particularly to farmers. That work is done by the Department of Agriculture, while the other work, related to the natural forests, is carried on by the Department of Mines and Resources. They will get their money for the special work that is to be done during the reconstruction period from the reconstruction vote. We will supply men who will cooperate with them in some of the work, but really the work will be carried on by the Department of Mines and Resources.
Those whom you might call research men, then, would be in the Department of Mines and Resources rather than in the Department of Agriculture?

We do the work in connection with breeding plants; we do the research work in connection with diseases of plants and in connection with attacks made "by insects upon plants, through our entomological branch. All that work is done by our research men, but they work in cooperation with the others.

A short time ago the hon. member for Swift Current raised a question I should like to pursue a little; that is, the possibility of using airports that have been declared surplus for experimental stations. As the minister probably knows, at Dauphin we have two very fine airports. It is possible that one may be used for commercial purposes, but at least one will be declared surplus. Has the department taken into consideration the possibility of using these airports that have been declared surplus for experimental stations, or anything of that sort? I might point Out that both the Dauphin airports are built on some of the finest land in Manitoba; they have fine buildings, water supply, electricity, and are close to town. Either one would make a fine experimental station. We have tried to get the Manitoba government interested in starting an agricultural college at one of these airports, but they have decided against it, so that I hope the dominion department will be able to make some use of these facilities.

If I may revert to the answer given by the minister a few minutes ago with respect to research in forestry, I was not aware that his department was doing as

much in the way of research along forestry lines as apparently is being done. Could the minister give the committee a general idea as to why any research is Joeing carried out by the Department of Reconstruction, when the Department of Agriculture apparently has men who can do it?	.

I do not like to be too specific in the matter, but I do not think it is the intention of the Department of Reconstruction actually to do any of this work. The principle, as I understand it, is this, that during the war we have been voting considerable sums of money for war purposes. If I wanted any of that money to develop something having to do with the war-possibly the greater production of hogs needed for food-I would have to go to the Minister of Finance who had charge of the fund and ask for a part of that money, through treasury board, to carry on the work. But that work was not carried out by the department which had control of the funds. They examined into the necessity for it, and if they thought it was necessary for the performance of part of the war effort the money would be turned over to the department in question carrying on the activity.
My understanding is that the Department of Reconstruction is going to take similar procedure in respect of a very considerable sum of money which may be voted by the house. Parliament will vote a sum of money. Then, for example, I would say that some irrigation work must be carried on in connection with research. This would be something outside and beyond anything provided by the civil estimates to my department. If I can convince them that the work I have suggested is important enough to make a sum of money available, we would then bring in a supplementary estimate which would propose to spend that money in the Department of Agriculture.
I think it would be also true to say that the Department of Mines and Resources would have to go to the Department of Reconstruction. The Department of Reconstruction would have the final say as to whether that money is to be used in a certain way, rather than by the Department of Agriculture, or somewhere else. But once the money is supplied for the work, our officials and those of the Department of Mines and Resources will carry it out.
For example, in connection with a dam required to promote irrigation, I understand that even after we have persuaded the Department of Reconstruction that we need the money and that the project is a good one,

Supply-Agriculture
it may say, "But you have not the proper engineering skill in your department to do this work." We would then say, "Whom do you recommend as engineer?" Or we might say, "If you have engineers elsewhere who you believe can do this work, who are they?" In this way we would cooperate in getting the work done. The work will be carried out by whatever department or branch has been accustomed to carrying it out in the past. In this instance it would be Mines and Resources, and Agriculture.

I can understand how engineering work might be handled in that way. But with a branch [DOT] of forestry in the Department of Mines and Resources, and with an experimental farms branch in the Department of Agriculture, in which there are experimental and research men, I. cannot understand why another department-a new one-should be undertaking work which already is being done in one or two other departments? At the moment I am not criticizing; I am only seeking to understand why such duplication is necessary.
May I have an answer to the question I asked a minute ago?
Up to this time no consideration has been given to using the airport at Dauphin. I do not know whether any consideration will be given to it or not.

Item agreed to.
15. Production service administration, $35,445

In the war appropriation estimates for the Department of Agriculture, as they are shown at page 552 of Hansard, there is a vote for subsidies amounting to $27,111,749 to producers of food products. May I ask about that item at this point?
Subsidies are paid to bring about greater production, and to that extent the item could be discussed now.
Would the minister give the committee a breakdown? What amount has been spent under this item on different agricultural products?

Perhaps I might be permitted to interject a brief observation at this point. I notice that, as we are reaching another branch of the work of the department, the minister is changing advisers. I should like to associate myself with those who have complimented the minister and his department upon the type of work which has been
done across Canada in the last thirty or forty or fifty years by the experimental farms branch. Anyone who is familiar with that service particularly in recent years, must realize that it has been a wonderful investment, one which has returned to this country manyfold the expenditures made in connection with it. I commend the whole service from top to bottom, and in this respect would include the minister as well.

I believe it is understood that certain subsidies ate given to increase production and others are given to offset the price ceiling. Would the minister make a full statement regarding marketing as well as production?

May I add a word in support of the hon. member for Haldimand. Could we have a general statement which w'ould give the full picture of subsidies administered by the minister's department? When we reach other departments we can get similar statements from them.
There is a lengthy list, but I could begin to give it.
I believe the hon. member for Haldimand was referirng to the fact that large items are spent by the Minister of Agriculture and other large items by the Minister of Finance. Is this true?

Some subsidies known as consumer subsidies are paid to cut down the cost of living. Then other subsidies are paid for the purpose of getting greater production, and consist in increased payments to producers. I believe that information can be supplied from the figures I have before-me. All are listed together in the information given me, but I believe when going through them they could be separated.
Is there any prepared . document giving that information?
The document I have gives it pretty well.
Have we had that document?

I doubt if you have,,
but it can be had. I have here the details of estimated expenditures for the fiscal year 1945-46, the one we are now in. For the agricultural food board the sum of $21,334 is-given for administration. That is the amount, already granted. The additional amount required is 840,695, making a total requirement for 1945-46 of $62,029. That is for administration.
Supply-Agriculture

Then follow subsidies on food products. The subsidy on milk for butter, fluid milk and cheese concentrates for 1944 was $4,500,000, and for this year, $4,500,000. The subsidy on milk for 1945:	amount already granted
$22,000,000; amount required, $23,000,000; total, $45,000,000. Subsidy to producers of fruits for jam and canned raspberries: 1945, $200,000 already granted, $400,000 still required, or $600,000 in all. Subsidies to producers of fruits for jam and canned raspberries, 1944, $83,333; and for this year it is $83,333. Subsidy to producers of tomatoes, corn, peas and beans: $200,000 already granted; $2,550,000 required, or a total in all of $2,7';0,000. Subsidy to producers of tomatoes, corn, peas and beans, 1944, $22,916,000. Subsidy to producers of white and yellow eyed beans:	$100,000 already
granted; $1,100,000 additional amount required, making a total of $1,200,000. Subsidy on milk used in the manufacture of lactose, $5,500. The total amount already granted, which includes some grants prior to this year, is $27,111,749. The total amount required to March 31, 1946, is $27,050,000. Total amount required-it says here for 1945-46 but I think that is the total down to the end of 1945-46, according to what I have been reading-is $54,161,749.

Would the Minister of
Agriculture have this information put in form and then place it on Hansard to-morrow the way it is given, because it is a little difficult to follow?

I could have a table made up and bring it in when we start the estimates again and ask to have it placed on Hansard. I take it that what is wanted is a total of subsidies paid right through the war period.
Yes.
Would the hon. member like that divided into producer subsidies and consumer subsidies?
All subsidies administered by the minister's department.
That would be only producer subsidies.
When we come to other -departments we can get the subsidies paid by ilhem and then have the whole picture.

I should like to know if the annual dominion-provincial production conference which was organized some years ago and which is representative of dominion and provincial departments of agriculture and farm organizations is to meet

to make an all-out effort to cooperate in the production of food. I think it is essential that this conference should meet- and that the techniques and cooperation which are provided be continued in the post-war period.

The conference is to be held on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of next week. This will be the first meeting after the war, and it is our intention to continue to hold them as long as we can secure the cooperation of the provinces and the farm organizations. Therefore I think they will continue right on through the years. We believe they are helpful and serve a good purpose.
I w'ould call the. attention of the leader of the opposition to the fact that a return is to brought down in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor) on October 7. The hon. member asked what amount had been paid in subsidies by the government from September 1, 1939, to September 15, 1945, and on what products were subsidies paid during that period and how much on each. This return I think could properly be put on Hansard, although it might be well to bring it up to date. It deals not only with the subsidies we have been dealing with but also with freight subsidies which work into the production of farm products. All kinds of subsidies are given and my hon. friend could very easily take out those that he has in mind.
That seems a good suggestion. If there is any item omitted in that return, perhaps the minister would see that it too is included on Hansard.
I think the part of the return which I have is an answer to those matters which concern agriculture, and it covers other subsidies which we have not discussed to-day.

I hold in my hand the proposals of the government of Canada to the dominion-provincial conference, and on page 9 I find the following:
To eliminate war-time subsidies related to the stabilization policy when inflationary pressures begin to ease.
What, if any, agricultural products would come under that clause? There must be some subsidies being paid by the Department of Agriculture which would come under that classification.

There will come a time. I do not know just how soon or how late, when we will transfer from the policy we have been following during the war to the policy provided under the legislation to establish floor prices which we passed at the last

Supply-A griculture
regular session. Under that the Department of Agriculture is provided with $200,000,000 to be used as a circulating fund to do during the transitional period following the war what we were doing under the War Measures Act during the war, that is, to carry on in principle the same kind of thing. When the time comes to discontinue the payment of subsidies under the war measure, then the board that has to do with the other measure will come into operation. Whatever conditions will have to be met, I anticipate, if it is necessary to use that fund, we will use it. The plan under which it will work is one of two ways. Either we will say to the people who are new in the business, whether cooperatives or persons in private business, "Go ahead and market the products," and if it is marketed at a price which is as high as or higher than we consider a reasonable floor, it will not be necessary to use any of the $200,000,000 by way of assistance. But if it is necessary to market the product at a lower return than that, then we will say to these parties, "Go ahead and market the product at whatever y.ou can get for it and you will be paid the difference between what you get and the floor price. In other words, you can proceed to pay the farmer the floor price and any difference between that and what you actually get for it will be refunded out of this fund." That is a subsidy, but it will not continue under the plan which has been followed during war1 time; it will be continued under the floor prices measure. Does that answer the question?
It does not answ* as to the specific products which will come under it.
I should have said that the $200,000,000 is provided for all products excepting grain.
Does that include barley, oats, flax or rye, or just wheat?

No; it leaves all the grain to the wheat board. The board which is set up for handling farm products under what we have come to call the floor prices measure has $200,000,000 for everything but grain. At the time the bill was discussed the government announced as a policy that similar provision of funds will be made to the wheat board when the time comes that that provision is required; a similar provision will be made to supply funds to the wheat board to do the same thing in relation to grain. In other words, the $200,000,000 is to operate outside of grain. It can be understood that \ye have had experiences in the past when it would have required perhaps the whole
$200,000,000 to handle grain. That was not considered a sufficient sum to take grain in, and it was provided at the time as part of the government's policy that if it became necessary, in order to maintain the proper floor level of grain, sufficient funds with which to do it would be made available to the wheat board.

Can we take it from the minister's remarks that it will be the policy of the government to see that, either under present subsidies or the floor price legislation, the prices of agricultural products are maintained at present levels as long as production costs remain at their levels as of the present time?

I would not want to say definitely that on every single farm product that would necessarily carry through, but I would say that that is the general principle underlying the policy. There may be some products-I am not prepared to say at the moment-to which we gave special consideration during war time because we required production for a special purpose during the war and may not require it for the same purpose during peace time, for instance, some of the oils which we required and of which we promoted the production because they could not be obtained at that time from the East Indies; it may not be advisable, all things considered, to try to persuade farmers to produce such products during peace time.

In that connection, if that is the policy of the government I cannot understand what has taken place with respect to the production of bacon in this country. The minister through the policies he has instituted has certainly caused the production of bacon to decrease greatly. He gave his policy in the house not very long ago, when he stated that as far as the production of bacon in western Canada was concerned, and I quote his words as reported in Hansard of September 24, at page 498:
This simply means that a farmer in the west must make a decision, and must have an argument with himself as to whether it pays best to feed barley or to sell it, and that is exactly the position in which we wanted him.
It seems to me that the production of hogs and bacon is an important part of our economy. It is something in which there is and has been a profit. It is an article which is needed. Yet the minister, through various types of legislation and the control of the price of grain, has reduced the profit on the production of that product, especially in western Canada, to a point where it is uneconomic at the present time. I have come from
Supply-Agriculture

tvhat I believe is the largest hog-producing district in Saskatchewan. More hogs have been raised in the Carrot river valley than anywhere else in Saskatchewan and, probably,, in the three western provinces, but a serious situation exists there at the present time. From observation I am sure there has been a reduction of production there of at least forty per cent; as yet the trend has not been stopped, and I am just wondering what steps, if any, the minister is taking to arrest that decline or to get people back to the production in western Canada of this important product.
I believe, given natural conditions, there is no other place in the world where pork can be produced cheaper than in western Canada. We grow the grain, and the hogs are raised on the farms where the grain is grown, so that the only freight which has to be paid, is the freight on the finished' product. But the policy which the government has adopted, of making it practically uneconomic to produce hogs there, is certainly creating a situation which I think should be remedied.

I wish to take just a moment or two, 'since it is six o'clock. The present position is that there is a reduction of fifteen per cent in the production of meat in Canada this year as compared with last year.
I was referring to hogs.
Grain is needed for one purpose just as much as for the other. If you are going to finish beef you finish it largely with grain-.	1
May I just point out to the minister-

I ask the hon. member to wait a moment if he wants a reply; if not,
I will sit down. The real reduction in meat in Canada is fifteen per cent, and it is to a large extent the same farmers who feed hogs who also feed cattle. Some farmers feed hogs and do not. feed' cattle; seme feed cattle and do not feed hogs; but, generally speaking, the hogs and cattle are both fed on the family-sized farms across Canada; they are not fed on the bigger ranches. About ten per cent only of the beef is fed there; the great proportion is fed on the small farms. The general situation is that you cannot have at this time more hogs in Canada than you have now. My hon. friends keep getting up and saying that the government has some policy which has resulted in there being fewer hogs. The government has not anything of the kind, and the government policy with regard to it has had very little to do with the matter, either when we had a big increase

or a considerable drop. I can remember when the opposition, sitting where they are now although there were not so many of them, used to tell us that we were taking credit for what providence had done. I [DOT] said at that time that I would much rather be with providence than against it. While we do not take all the credit for increasing the production, may I point out that if our hon. friends thought increased production should1 follow the good weather of 1942, they should, in accordance with that same idea, agree that when the production of grain is not so great, we cannot have as high a production of live stock. Let me put on the record the figures for the carryover of oats at the end of the year. From 1935 to 1939 the average carryover was 35,000,000 bushels at the end of the crop year. The average from 1940 to 1944 was 85,000,000 bushels. Even after we had fed greater, numbers of live stock we still had a carryover of 85,000.000 bushels. For the year 1944-45, ended July last, the carryover was 98,000,000 bushels, after we had fed more live stock and exported grain. For 1945-46 we estimate that it will be 46,000,000 bushels, and for 1946-47 it is estimated that it will be 25.000,000 bushels. Our production of live stock goes up and down with the production of grain, and the production of grain goes up and down with the weather, as everyone knows who has been on a farm; particularly is that so where grain growing is the main activity.
With regard to barley, the situation is much the same. The carryover at the end of the year, for the period from 1935 to 1939, was 9,000,000 bushels; from 1940 to 1944 it was
33.000.	000 bushels; for 1944-45 it was 29,000,000 bushels; and for 1945-46 it is estimated at
15.000.	000 bushels. It is estimated that we may have an increase in barley because of the increased acreage in 1946-47.
The policy of the government has been to study these figures, to encourage the production of feed grain and to estimate what is going to happen on the basis of grain production. When hon. members in the early part of the war were getting up cohtinually and saying that next year we would have a decrease in production we kept continually saying, "No; we are not." The only reason wp had for that statement was that our statisticians were able to assure us that there was such a condition prevailing on the land across Canada that we would have an increased production of feed grain, and as we had an increased production of feed grain the farmers would feed more live stock. In order to make sure that we would have enough we paid $4 an acre to take land out of wheat and put it into feed

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
grain and summer fallow for the purpose of increasing grain production. , That was our policy and we got wheat acreage down from
28,000,000 acres to 17,000,000 acres and summer fallow acreage up by 6,000,000 acres, while oats and barley acreage was up. In 1942 we produced twice as much feed grain as in any other year.
I am quite prepared to agree with hon. members who point out that at that time the weather had a lot to do with the matter, but the weather has had a lot) to do with cutting down production since. Hon. members have been telling us for three years that we have had a drought on the boundary line between Saskatchewan and Alberta.
You did not raise hogs there.

We raised hogs there in -1942-43. My hon. friend was sitting in the 'legislature when the money was voted to take hogs into that part of the country, and a great part of our increased production came from that dried-out area as well as from other areas where there was an increase. With the drought of 1943 some of these men went out of hogs. With the drought of 1944 more . went out of hogs, and with the drought of this year still more have gone out of hogs. Live stock is still there, with the result that one member asked me this afternoon how we would provide feed for the live stock in view of the fact that with the early coming of winter live stock cannot be fed in that section of the country at present.
The problem has always been one, first, for the provincial governments, add when they have not enough grain in their own province to move into dried-out areas within their own boundary lines they have come to us and asked us to provide grain out of some other province. We have cooperated with the governments in the freezing of grain in those areas, and it is the freezing of grain in those areas to complete the feeding of hogs that has made it possible for the farmers to produce the numbers coming from there now. The method of freezing grain there was simply to tell the farmers to sell that grain for feeding hogs instead of selling it to- make beer. We said, "You will get the same -price for grain to feed hogs as you would have got for grain for brewing purposes." Because we did that we are getting higher production than otherwise. I wish to repeat that much of the reduction is due to the fact that we have not had very favourable weather in- the last two or three, years. Our grain production is down.

The minister will recall
that on different occasions 'in this house I pointed out that from a sow that went over the butcher's block you would not raise a litter of pigs.

That is quite true; no
sow that goes over the butcher's block will raise a litter of pigs. But my hon. friend knows, as I know, that a contented sow feeds much more easily than one which is not contented, and there are many sows that go over the block which were not intended to raise litters of pigs. One cannot take statistics with regard- to sows that go over the block and base conclusions upon it. The basis of feeding all live stock is grain, and the policy which the government intends to lay before the provinces next Monday is the policy of the war years of producing more feed grain in order that we may get more hogs and cattle. Without more feed grain we cannot finish even the hogs and cattle we now have.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, November 27, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Maedonnell (Muskoka-Ontario), and on the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when eleven o'clock came last night I was just about to sum up what I had been trying to say in the budget debate. I had advanced certain principles which I thought should be embodied in a national budget that would be adequate to meet the economic conditions of our time. In my concluding remarks I wish to advance the idea that the time has come when the Canadian people will have to make a great decision, and that decision will be the matter of deciding the framework within which we intend to develop democracy.
Last night I tried to show that it is not possible to develop a true democracy within the framework of capitalism or so-called free
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

enterprise. The profit motive itself is entirely undemocratic. The relationships which the conflicts in the industrial field produce between the employer and the employee are undemocratic. The relationship which exists to-day between the great monopolies and the farming industry is undemocratic. The profit motive is undemocratic because it cannot be universalized. You can universalize the ballot to every person of a certain age; that is democratic. You cannot universalize profit because it is not possible for everyone to make profit. It is only possible for a privileged few to make profits, and they must be made at the expense of the great majority of the people. Therefore the relationships which the present system leaves amongst people is entirely democratic.
These are some of the things to which we must give a great deal more attention than we have hitherto been accustomed to do. I suggest that the great democratic ideal which this country held throughout the years of war should be the objective in time of peace. It is true that in the war years our democratic ideals were more or less negative. We were in a struggle to retain that measure of democracy which we had achieved, and that itself was worth fighting for, but it was negative. The time has come for us to make a positive effort to build a true and real democracy in this country. With regard to the budget in that respect I would suggest to the minister that the budget should be prepared for at least a five-year period instead of from year to year, thus giving the government an opportunity to carry out its own policy. As I understand it, this policy is to entrust the affairs of the nation to private enterprise, and when private enterprise breaks down, as everybody believes it will break down, then the government is going to enter into fairly extensive public expenditures to take up the slack which will result from failures of private enterprise. If that is to be done, and if we are to be protected from the swings from booms to slumps, then a five-year period would be the better basis of a budget, and would leave the government a better opportunity to protect itself and to protect the country from the failures of private enterprise.
I wish to make just one more observation in relation to War Assets Corporation and the surplus goods in their hands. In particular, I desire to make a remark about the surplus goods which could be used for educational purposes. Such goods have already been paid for by the Canadian people. I deplore the idea of passing these goods into the hands of the manufacturers, and then having them 
sell them again* to the Canadian public. All goods which can be used in public institutions, such as our educational institutions, should be given to these schools and colleges absolutely free. The same idea applies to medical institutions, hospitals, and so forth, and also to materials which were used in dramatics. They could be distributed also to communities to be used in the interests of art and for the recreation of the general public.
Then we have a great demand from farmers and communities for equipment which is now being declared surplus. For instance, the people of Dawson Creek want to purchase a road-grader from the R.C.A.F. I have not been able to have that done for them. The government refuses to consider their application; the chances are that the road-graders there will be sent in to the control of War Assets Corporation, shipped out of the country, and sold for a song to the big interests, and these people will never have a chance to purchase it at all. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything on the budget, and even now I rise merely to make a few comments in order to clarify the stand of this group on the two amendments which are before the house.
As the house is well aware, only two amendments may be moved on the budget. Therefore we in this group find ourselves at this time in the position of being unable to move an amendment. Consequently we have to take a definite stand on the amendments that are now before the house. First of all, I wish to refer to the amendment moved by the C.C.F.
I should like to refer to page 2565 of Hansard and quote what the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had to say with reference to the amendment moved by the Conservative party. I quote as follows:
... I am going to move an amendment; for although we of the C.C.F. could vote for the words of the amendment, we cannot vote for what we believe to be the substance of the speech which introduced it or what lies behind the words of the amendment.
No doubt the leader of the C.C.F. party was perfectly justified in taking that attitude; but since he has done so in reference to the Conservative amendment. I am sure he will not object to the members of this group applying the same sort of reasoning to his own amendment. If w*e take the C.C.F. amendment and apply to it that kind of reasoning,
I want to ask the house just exactly what we have. I am satisfied that if you asked every

The Budget-Mr. Quelch
hon. member to say exactly what the C.C.F. amendment means, under that sort of reasoning, probably you would get as many different answers as there are members. I would not hesitate to say that this amendment not only denotes but connotes complete socialization of industry in progressive stages. I should like to read the first part of the amendment; that is the only part to which I intend to refer. It is found on page 2566 of Hansard'.
That the amendment be amended by adding to paragraph (a) the -words, "which require the use of our national credit in terms of public need . . ."
I should like to pause there for a moment, because it is interesting to note these words. ". . . to make possible a large-scale investment programme, the public reconversion of war industries for peace-time needs, the public development of new industries, of scientific research and of our natural resources."
You will note, Mr. Speaker, in the amendment the word "public"; "the public reconversion of war industries for peace-time needs, the public development of new industries, of scientific research and of our natural resources," so that I think everyone will agree that this amendment at least must mean that war industries changed over to the production of peace-time goods will be nationalized or socialized or publicly owned or however you

The original section submitted to the convention and which drew opposition from delegates Harold Winch, C.C.F. house leader in the British Columbia legislature, and convention chairman Colin Cameron, of Courtenay, B.C., urged:
