"We are now a strong political force in Canada," he said, "and we are on the eye of winning power. We must think in responsible terms as if we were in power."
A motion by Mr. K. Han, a C.C.F. candidate in West York, to have the section,replaced by a section of the Regina manifesto was defeated by an overwhelming majority of the delegates after he stated that Mr. Lewis wanted "power at any cost," and that the present motion had been drafted for the sake of political expediency.

I was saying that in mj' constituency a few years ago. there was a good deal of interest in regard to the possibilities of cooperation between progressive groups. Speaking at a meeting, I stated that as far as the C.C.F. were concerned they only believed in the socialization of monopolistic institutions. A C.C.F. supporter in the back of the hall got up and demanded that I withdraw that statement. He said it was an absolute misinterpretation of the C.C.F. stand, that they stood for absolute socialization of all industry. You find that attitude in many places, especially in the west, even if that is not the attitude in the east. But where there is smoke there is fire, and I suppose there must be some reason for this dispatch from the Montreal convention. I should not think the press entirely imagined it; there must have been some, reason for making a statement of that kind.
However, Mr. Speaker, let us go to western Canada. I should like to go to Calgary instead of Montreal because. I think Calgary is a more progressive city; and perhaps the C.C.F. will be more satisfied with this quotation. It is dated November 11, 1943, and appeared in the Calgary Herald, referring to a speech made there by Mr. Winch. I am not going to quote the whole speech; I wish to quote only that part relative as to whether or not the C.C.F. stands for full socialism, or pink socialism or red socialism or whatever it may be. So that I am going to quote only
fMr. Quelch.]
that part; I am not going to quote the rest of it; I am sure the C.C.F. would take great exception to it:
Mr. Winch declared that if and when his party assumes power at Ottawa it will institute socialism immediately.
That seems pretty definite and I do not think it has ever been denied. So again I say that if we use the reasoning toward the C.C.F. amendment as suggested by the leader of the C.C.F. party in connection with the Progressive Conservative amendment, then we are bound to come to the conclusion that this amendment means the socialization of all industry in Canada-maybe not to-morrow, maybe gradually and in stages, so much this year and so much next year. But I think most hon. members will agree the last general election showed clearly that the people of Canada were turning thumbs down on socialism at this time: If there is any doubt about that so far as some parts of Canada are concerned, certainly there can be no doubt as far as Alberta is concerned. The people of that province have turned thumbs down doubly in so. far as the C.C.F. programme is concerned, first at the provincial election and then at the federal one.
I should like to say a few words about the amendment offered by the Progressive Conservative party, and I shall do as was suggested by the leader of the C.C.F., namely, follow the same line of reasoning as they followed. But before leaving the C.C.F. amendment, I might add that in view of the fact that it definitely does stand for the complete socialization of industry, this group will be voting against it.
So far as the Progressive Conservative amendment is concerned, I would turn to page 1302 of Hansard and read the amendment as it appears on that page:
The house regrets:
(a)	That no effective plan has been proposed to ensure full production and employment;
(b)	That no satisfactory policy has been advanced for the elimination of extravagant governmental expenditures.
Just exactly what is the stand of the Progressive Conservative party, so far as governmental expenditures are concerned? If we would turn to page 1296 of Hansard we would get a pretty' good idea where they stand in this regard. This is what we find:
So far as expenditure is concerned we must make up our minds, based on the best estimate we can make of the national income, how much of this income can be safely taken by the state; and having made up our minds on this, we must then make a heroic effort to keep our expenditure within that amount.
That is to say, we must first of all decide upon the amount of money we can obtain

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
from the people by taxation, and then curtail our expenditures down to the amount of money we obtain. In other words, it is a proposal that we return to the pre-war financial policy of the Liberal government, and attempt to balance the budget. It is the same old policy of belt-tightening that we had in the thirties.
This group has always taken a definite stand against that kind of policy, and therefore we will find it necessary to vote against the Progressive Conservative amendment.
Since the government apparently proposes to continue its policy in regard to debt finance we will also be voting against the main motion. So that we^will be voting against all three-the two amendments and the main motion before the house.
If we had been in a position to move an amendment, all we would have found it necessary to do would be to strike out the word "public" from the two places in which it occurs in the amendment offered by the C.C.F. party.
I refer to the word "public" where it appears before the words "reconversion" and "development". But the C.C.F. party inserted that word for a definite reason, namely, so that we might possibly be embarrassed in voting against the remainder of the amendment to the amendment.

The group to which I belong believes in a pay-as-you-go policy. That is the stand we have taken consistently ever since we came here in 1935. Our stand has always been that to the extent that taxation fails to meet government expenditures, national money should be utilized1. In this way the people of Canada may be given the highest standard of living of which the country is capable, without increasing our public debt.
During the war it will be remembered that. no financial restrictions were allowed to impede our war effort. Unfortunately, however, already there are signs which show that our standard of living in the future is to be governed by certain artificial monetary limitations. That is why we are opposing the main motion before the house.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now almost three months since I first entered this chamber as member for the federal constituency of Moose Jaw. The current budget materially affects the wellbeing of my constituents and the people of Saskatchewan generally. Therefore, before it is passed I should like to make a few observations.
Speaking in parliament last September 20 the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. McGarry) made a plea with which I am entirely in accord. Addressing the government he said:
Do not forget that you cannot have absolute peace in Canada while there is one section which is discriminated against.
I would suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has apparently overlooked that admonition in the preparation of his budget. Once again, it seems to me, my province is a forgotten unit. In the past, one federal government after another has overlooked the vital needs of Saskatchewan. The present administration, unless it alters some of its major policies, will perpetuate serious economic injustices.	,
To-day, despite what the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) said last evening, there is a high degree of resentment in western Canada over the fact that westerners have not yet been given economic equality with the people of central Canada. They are in fact being discriminated against in an economic way. If their grievances are not rectified, then sooner or later I believe the harmony of confederation may be disrupted.
The economic problems of the maritime provinces are similar to those we have on the prairies. I listened with interest some weeks ago to the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) voice some of those grievances. Perhaps if all hon. members from the west and all from the maritimes, regardless of party affiliation, could get together for a few days we might be able to persuade the the administration that we are serious when we say that there is something wrong in our respective sections, and that we would like something to be done about those wrongs.
The first grievance in Saskatchewan for forty years has been the Canadian tariff structure. In times of depression and prosperity alike, the dead-weight of the tariff has borne more heavily upon my province, the one least able to bear it. than on any other province in Canada. Citizens of Saskatchewan, indeed citizens of Canada generally are indignant when they compare the prices of many articles in the United States with the prices of the same articles in Canada.
For years the government have been committed to a policy of freer trade. They have taken numerous steps in that direction. Yet the hard fact remains that the people of Western Canada are still paying exorbitant prices for hundreds of articles which they obtain from the United States.
In order to illustrate that point, with the permission of the house I should like to table
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher

a .record of the tariff on ten articles as taken from the customs tariff and amendments of January 20, 1944. May I do that, Mr. Speaker?

Those charges totalled $40.06. or 66-5 per cent of the original cost. Hon. members can see how adversely our cost of living is affected by the tariff.
We resent the tariff because it is purely and simply a form of taxation imposed by certain interests, for the most part in central Canada, on the rest of the people. It gives those interests the power to tax others to such a degree that, in many cases, of every dollar spent by a maritimer or a westerner, twenty-five cents is a direct tribute to the industrialist of central Canada.
For years our people have been compelled to purchase their necessities for the most part in a high-cost protected market. They have had no alternative. The tariff, has virtually bonused the industry' of central Canada.
Westerners compare such bonusing with the treatment which agriculture, their chief industry, has received. During the W'orld depression when prices of farm products dropped to unbelievably low levels, our farmers for the most part were forced to accept those competitive world prices. With the outbreak of war, when food became scarcer prices began
[Mr. Thaletur.l
to go up. It looked as though at long last they might reach a reasonable level. However. before they were allowed to reach that level, in most cases they were frozen by the administration. In other words, the western farmer for almost all his products has been and still is denied competitive world prices. When world markets were low for the most part he was given no aid. I think that will be sufficient to establish -what I am trying to point, out. This report shows that United States live stock prices are as much as forty-five per cent higher than similar Canadian prices. Western farmers are indignant over the government's continued refusal to allow them to take advantage of this higher market.
It is the same story with wheat. Hon, members will remember what happened on the floor of this house not very many weeks ago. The government suddenly announced one afternoon that the export price of wheat, No. 1 northern, basis Fort William, would have a ceiling of SI.55 from that time forward. The world price of wheat is approximately S2 and there is every indication that it may go higher, which means that every

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
time a farmer in western Canada sells a bushel of wheat he is penalized approximately forty-five cents in hard cash.
We in Saskatchewan resent this policy. We feel that the government is playing Santa Claus with our money without our consent. If the national interest; if the interest of Canada as a -whole, demands that wheat be sold to the people of Europe at forty-five cents less than world market prices, then the people of Canada as a whole should finance that difference and not the farmers of the 'west who can least afford to, and who have had no say in the making of the gift. The crux of the issue is this: While the industry of central Canada has been highly protected for years, virtually bonused by the tariff, the chief industry in my province, agriculture, not only has received no protection, but has actually been penalized by government action. We can neither buy our necessities in the United States markets, where we can purchase them cheaper, nor can we sell our agricultural products in the United States, where we could obtain much more. I suggest that that is scarcely economic justice; rather it seems' to me to be economic discrimination.
I strongly criticize the current budget for its treatment of the tariff question. It has failed completely to alleviate the present hardships caused, by the tariff. Indeed originally,, it actually attempted to increase them. Higher tariffs were put on several items. The fact that public pressure later caused the government to withdraw those increases does not alter its original intention. The government did not withdraw the tariff on diesel engines. I understand that that tariff was put on by order in council, without any discussion by the tariff board, and certainly without any discussion in this house. In view of the professed trade policy of the government, westerners find it hard to understand its actions.
In countless public utterances, both in and out of parliament, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and numerous of his cabinet ministers have declared their intention of working toward freer trade and lower tariffs. Permit me to quote some of their statements. Our Prime Minister is reported in Maclean's magazine of February 1, 1945, as having stated:
The Liberal party stands for the removal of harriers to trade, and is opposed to the principle of protection, which is really a levy on consumers in Canada as well as on all export industries for the benefit of protected industries
What the government favours is the progressive removal, in association with other nations, of tariff and other restrictive devices for protecting particular industries.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) is reported as having said at a foreign trade convention in New York on October 26, 1943:
I find myself more and more attached to the approach of a ceiling on tariffs, no ceiling on trade, a ceiling on all trade restrictions.
The Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), in a white paper of the government on reconstruction, tabled in>
this house last April, stated, among other things:
Nor is the contraction of Canadian imports any part of the government's employment policy.
In short the government has been committed by numerous statements of cabinet ministers to the rejection of a high tariff policy. Yet in the current budget there is no attempt to translate these lofty words into concrete facts. The same government which has been preaching free trade for many years; the same government which only three years ago signed a document with the United States subscribing to the policy of lowering tariff barriers, now, in its first budget, actually attempted to raise the tariff in several instances.
The protective tariff has developed in central Canada a large industrial empire, but I would suggest that in doing so it has often proved harmful to the other provinces.
For many years protectionists have used the argument that the tariff was needed to protect "baby industries" while they are making a beginning. We feel that it is about time the "baby industries" grew up and stood on their feet to meet outside competition.
In years past speakers from all major parties, representing the western constituencies, have spoken in favour of lower tariffs-and I include in that category the Prime Minister and the ministers of agriculture. The people in the outlying parts of the country cannot and will not continue to bonus eastern industry at such heavy cost. Tariff reduction is a matter of national urgency. Let the government take action while there is yet time.
Perhaps the second major grievance of my province is the inequitable railway rate structure. In 1937, according to a submission of the Saskatchewan government to the Sirois commission, local railway rates in the west ranged from forty-six to seventy per cent higher than in central Canada. They have not materially altered since that time. From the beginning of settlement this high cost of transport has hindered the development of the prairies, and if it is not soon lowered it will plague the post-war planners. Permit me to illustrate this point with some figure?.
The freight rate for 100 pounds of lumber moving from Megantic, Quebec, to Ingersoll, Ontario, a distance of 596 miles, is 24 cents;
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher

yet the freight rate on 100 pounds of lumber moving from Golden, British Columbia, to my own city of Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, also a distance of 596 miles, is 40J cents. In like manner the freight rate on 100 pounds of canned goods from Hamilton, Ontario, to a point in New Brunswick 800 miles away is 61-i cents; yet the freight rate from Fort William to Moose Jaw, a distance of 818 miles, on 100 pounds of canned goods is $1.04. The average rate on butter per 100 pounds in carloads from stations in Ontario and Quebec to Montreal is about 60 cents; yet butter from Moose Jaw, to reach the Toronto and Montreal market in carloads, must pay $2.05 per 100 pounds. These differences are not isolated cases. Hundreds more could be easily quoted. They are typical of the freight situation as it exists to-day in Canada.
Besides such' inequalities in the general rate structureJ there are certain special discriminations which have long caused heart-burnings in the western provinces. One of these is the "water-compelled" rates from eastern Canada to points on the British Columbia coast, caused by the competition of ships going through the Panama canal.
These "water-compelled" rates often mean that it costs more to ship goods from eastern Canada to many points on the prairies than it does to ship them from the east to points on the Pacific coast. As was pointed out this morning by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), the cost of sending 100 poupds of barbed wire from Montreal to Calgary is $1.98; yet the cost of sending 100 pounds of barbed wire from Montreal to Vancouver is only 95 cents, even though the latter is a thousand mile longer trip.

speechtext: It should be 75 cents.

speechtext:
I believe it was changed some weeks ago, and it is now 95 cents. Similarly, the cost of sending 100 pounds of paint from Montreal to Calgary is $1.98; yet the cost of sending 100 pounds of paint from Montreal to Vancouver is only $1.50. The prairie provinces are obliged to pay higher freight charges in order that the railways may give British Columbia coastal points rates competitive with water transport. I am not saying that the rates to British Columbia are too low; we think they are the right ones; but we also think points on the prairies should have the advantage of the same rates.
The government should take action to prevent the railroads from charging higher rates to intermediate inland points than they charge to coastal points. Such a ruling, I might say, has existed in the United States

since 1914, and the result is reflected in a much more equitable distribution of industry throughout the western states.
Confederation originally, I believe, was meant to be an association of provinces equal in every respect. Confederation in fact has given the provinces political equality, but I do not believe that so far it has given us economic equality, and I suggest that the railway rate structure of this country is a glaring example of that failure. We in Saskatchewan are forced to pay higher freight rates than other parts of the country. Our standard of living is adversely affected in proportion to the difference. In addition, the higher freight rates are one of the chief reasons for Saskatchewan's lack of industrial growth. New industries are handicapped from the beginning, in meeting eastern competition, by the excessive rates. The Canadian railway rate structure makes extremely difficult industrial development except in one section of the country, a strip of territory lying between Montreal and Windsor. If confederation is to mean true economic equality for Saskatchewan, freight rates in the west must come down to the level of those in central Canada. Piecemeal adjustments will not suffice.
The people of Saskatchewan will also be disappointed that the administration has not seen fit to embark on any major irrigation projects at the present time. Year after year, great quantites of good water go to Hudson bay, from the prairies. Just a few million dollars spent putting it on our rich lands would pay dividends many times over.
The three factors which I have briefly touched upon-high tariffs, high freight rates, and lack of irrigation-have all contributed to make Saskatchewan a province almost without industries.
In 1942, a war year, in the whole province only 9,800 persons were engaged in manufacturing. Compare this with the number of persons employed in manufacturing industries in some of the other provinces.

Quebec	 400,000
British Columbia	 90,000

In 1939, only 1-81 per cent of all Canadian industrial production took place in my province. Our whole economy has been tied to the production of wheat, and the income of the province is subject to the vagaries of weather, and to the violent fluctuations of world prices.
Saskatchewan will probably always remain primarily agricultural, and yet the establishment and development of secondary industries would go a long way toward stabilizing our economy. The major problem facing this

The Budget-Mr. Hamel
country to-day is the provision of jobs for hundreds of thousands of returning servicemen. Saskatchewan wants to play her part in providing some of these jobs; yet in order to do so she must have a large growth of her industrial capacity.
The Saskatchewan government has realized that fact and has taken some steps to remedy the situation. It has built a woollen mill in Moose Jaw, a shoe factory in Regina, and a brick plant at Estevan, as well as several fish filleting plants. But these industries, while they are certainly a step in the right direction, are only a start. If Saskatchewan is to have any substantial industrial growth, the basic factors which work against that development must be removed.
No one in this house can blame the people of the west for seeking relief from these twin burdens of the tariff and high freight rates. This is not a western problem alone; it is a Canadian problem. History has always shown, I believe, that when the west is prosperous the rest of Canada is prosperous. If this government by its policies sentences the prairies to remain tied to a strictly wheat economy, I suggest that all the people of this nation face another economic tragedy.
I appeal to the federal government: first, to establish parity between the Canadian and the United States dollar; sepond, to take -action to bring freight rates prevailing in the western provinces down to the level of Ontario rates; third, to begin large scale irrigation programmes in western Canada as part of post-war rehabilitation plans; fourth, to bring about drastic tariff reforms.
To-day, as never before, every nation appears to be standing at the cross-roads. Trade rivalries are already chilling the friendships that existed between allied nations during the war. The world to-day is crying for leadership, and as one of the world's foremost trading nations Canada, I suggest, is well equipped to give that leadership. Tariff changes cannot be brought about if each nation waits for the other to make the first move. I believe that the federal government should immediately, or as soon as possible, make proposals to the United States and to all the nations of the British commonwealth to slash drastically trade barriers between their respective countries. If such proposals were successful other nations could later be included. Canada should give leadership in promoting freer trade. If these steps are taken by the administration I am sure that at long last the west will receive economic justice, and, moreover that the people of Canada will emerge a more united nation. I am sure also that if such steps are taken this country will be a better place in which to live.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of the budget debate, I should like to make a few remarks upon some problems which, to my mind, are important. I shall cover three points: 1. The present taxation system. 2. Unemployment. 3. The army.
1.	As regards the present taxation system, may I say that the Income Tax Act, as it now stands, provides that an employer must deduct at the source 95 per cent of the income tax payable by his employee. The tax is calculated not on the income for the whole year, but on what was earned during a given pay period, that is one week, two weeks or one month, according to. the method of payment followed by the employer.
In my humble opinion such a system entails two very serious points of discrimination:
(a) While in theory the employer retains but 95 per cent of the tax payable by his employee, it is found in practice that by the end of the year he has retained much more than what the employee actually owed. It is easy to understand how this can. happen.
An employee may earn S40 for one week, while drawing only S20 the following week, and losing a full week's salary afterwards. It might be argued that a readjustment is made at the end of the year. I say that statistics show that no such readjustment takes place.
During 1943-44 the government had to refund in 930,471 cases taxes that had wrongly been deducted at the source. In 1944-45 they had to make 1,041,264 refunds. The income tax is already so high and weighs heavily enough on the men in the lower salary brackets that no one should go as far as deducting more than they have to pay. When a legislation harms but a small number of people, it can be said that it is a necessary evil and that it is in the public interest, but when the harm is done to more than one million people, it behooves the government to rectify such a system. It should be noted that the huge number of 1,041,264 includes but the refunds which have actually been made by the income tax collector, but the number of justified applications submitted by ratepayers perhaps reaches two million, although no official figures are available.
Without vouching for its accuracy, I venture to suggest this figure which is based on the many complaints I have received from taxpayers in my constituency of Saint-Mau-rice-Lafleche.
Ob) The second unfair feature of the present system concerns all taxpayers since it entails heavy and useless expense on the part of the treasury. The figures speak for themselves. Last year, the government refunded over one million dollars. This means that the income
The Budget-Mr. Hamel

tax collector received over one million letters, that a corresponding number of files were brought out and checked, that over one million cheques were printed and as many envelopes addressed or at least sealed.
Supposing that one man spends half an hour on each case, this means that the government must occupy 300 employees at refunding amounts collected in excess. By taking SI,800 as the average annual salary of such an employee. I find that these refunds cost the treasury anywhere from 8500,000 to $600,000 a year. These figures, Mr. Speaker, are no indication of the trouble or expense to which the taxpayer has been put nor of the various calls he may have had to make, nor do they give any idea of the hardship inflicted on small wage earners by this unfair deduction which is refunded only two or three years later.
Mr. Speaker, among the various ways of improving on this situation, I shall insist on the following:
1.	Forsake the method of deduction at the source, as far as the small wage earner is concerned.
2.	Allow him at the beginning of the year to draw up an estimate of his earnings and to authorize his employer to deduct the amount he thinks will be expected of him, letting him make any required adjustment at the end of the year.
3.	Collect only 50 per cent instead of deducting 95 per cent at the source.
To my mind these three somewhat radical methods would greatly help in removing the rank injustice actually inflicted on small wage earners.
Now I should like to say a word in regard to unemployment which threatens our country and more particularly my own constituency. Two war plants have closed down, one at La Tuque, almost a year ago, and the other at Shawinigan. The workers of Shawimgan, Grand'Mere and La Tuque are greatly affected by this shut-down. If those plants cannot be used by large industries, I suggest that they be turned over to the municipal corporations which, in cooperation with the chambers of commerce, will find some means of using them in the interests of small industries. Action along those lines has already been taken at Granby and in the wonderful town of Grand-Mere and the results were conclusive.
However, as unemployment is a -basic economic problem among other problems which are perhaps just as fundamental, I do not propose to discuss it further to-night.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word in regard to demobilization and deserters.

The war in Europe has ended over six months ago and the war with Japan almost four months ago, and a large number of young men are still held in military camps where they are wasting their time. Eight out of ten service men whom I have met have stated that they do absolutely nothing useful in the army.
A large number have requested their discharge but they were told that they did not have enough points. I suggest that this policy be dropped and that the request of all those young men who apply for their discharge be granted immediately. I say, Mr. Speaker, all those who request their discharge, for I would not advocate a policy which would throw into, the streets hundreds of thousands of men who to-morrow might swell the ranks of the unemployed.
But when a soldier wishes to be demobilized and take his chances on life and the future, we have no right to deprive him of that opportunity. I would also add that the present reestablishment policy is unfair to the returned man who has complied1 with the legislation of his country. In my humble opinion, the problem of reestablishment is the same for all, no matter where they may have served. With the exception of those who have been wounded or have laid down their lives, and for whom I would be satisfied with asking for more generous allowances, the sane and fair basis for computing the reestablishment grants should be mainly the length of service. The financial losses of our soldiers are not determined by the place where they have served but by the length of their stay in the army. Whether I have mounted guard on the water front at Vancouver or on the shores of England, after four years of absence, I would naturally have lost my pre-war business; the loss of salary due to my leaving a job would be the same no matter what theatre of war I nlay have been sent to. The financial losses being similar, the reestablishment grants should be identical.
I now conclude, Mr. Speaker. In the course of the present session the case of the deserters has been mentioned time and again. Answers to various questions seem to indicate that the greatest number of them are to be found in the province of Quebec. This fact is no surprise to me, on the contrary, I wonder why there have not been more of them. Mr. Speaker, if the ordinary criminal is entitled to claim for his defence justifying excuses and extenuating circumstances, I hope that the same right will no.t be denied these young people who, in most cases, are merely the victims of mistakes made by certain public

The Budget-Mr. Hamel
men and, I might say, more especially by the party in power. I shall not undertake to remind the house of the various political movements launched in Quebec from 1919 to the present time. I shall be content to point out that from 1919 to 1939 the Liberal party have shown a tremendous zeal in promoting, in our province, a current of thought opposed to militarism and participation. Even in 1938, the French-Canadian members of the Liberal cabinet promised the electors of Lot-biniere and another Montreal constituency. St. Henri, I believe, that our country would abstain completely from any participation in a foreign war. And I say without fear of contradiction, that the advantage secured by the Liberal party over their Conservative opponents, in .Quebec, is almost solely due to this stand against participation. I must also state that at that time, the military policy of the C.C.F. party was the same.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) stated:
In the event of war, Canada's maximum contribution would be supplying of foodstuffs and material and under no circumstances would conscription be instituted to provide an expeditionary force overseas.
Even in the 1940 election, after Canada had declared war. it was claimed that participation would be kept on a voluntary basis.
I wish to quote a statement made by the leader of the Conservative party, who at that time was the Hon. Mr. Manion. I take this quotation from the March 5, 1940 issue of Le Devoir. Here is what the Hon. Mr. Manion had to say during that election campaign, on article 3 of his platform:
To my mind, conscription has failed in the last war because it resulted in the mobilization of 10,000 men only out of a total of_ over half a million and it caused disunion in this country.
For the above-mentioned reason, that is because conscription is not necessary in this war and because it is the duty of a public man to maintain our national unity, as I have stated on other occasions, I am entirely opposed to conscription. I made that clear on March 30 last, that is a year ago, in the House of Commons, and in the press, even before Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Lapointe had made their statements against conscription.	_
I have publicly expressed that view in this election campaign long before my arrival in the province of Quebec . . .
Canada has voluntarily entered this war as a sovereign nation and will voluntarily continue the struggle . . .
The formidable battle which the liberal party has always waged against a compulsory system of enrolment has brought about a change of heart among the Conservatives in parliament and elsewhere in the country.	.
It is up to the people to decide whether they will place their trust in these last-minute ( converts . . .
The Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe was claiming that he had turned the Conservatives against conscription.
... or & those who have always advocated the same policy and opposed a compulsory system of enrolment.
I solemnly declared in the House of Commons that not only would I refuse to be a member of a government that might enact conscription, but that I would oppose any government that tried to pass such a piece of legislation. I am still of the same mind and have expressed a similar opinion all over Canada.
Mr. Speaker, those words uttered by the various political leaders were spread by all the speakers of the various political parties, and they were quoted by the newspapers in all provinces. Eventually conscription was imposed.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I do not hesitate to say in view of those facts that those young men who have been reluctant to report and even those who have deserted were the victims of a mistake. There might be differences of opinion as to whether the mistake occurred at the time it was promised that conscription would'not be resorted to or when this promise was broken. But I believe that it will be recognized that a mistake has been made. And due to this mistake, some young men are now serving sentences of several months' detention and their wives and children are suffering hardships. The provincial or municipal authorities may be compelled to provide for a large number of those families in distress.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to ask the government to grant, as soon as' possible, an amnesty to all deserters to enable them to make a fresh start.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Resolved that it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act, and to provide
1. That for 1945 and subsequent taxation years the capital element in contractual annuities be exempt from tax.

May I congratulate the minister and the government on the fact that at last they have seen the wisdom and the equity of separating the capital element from the income element in annuity payments. I should like also to tender my thanks to the commission that sat on taxation of annuities and family corporations. Mr. William C. Ives, retired Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Alberta; Doctor D. A. MacGibbon of Winnipeg, and Mr. M. W. Mackenzie, formerly of Montreal and now Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, constituted that commission, and I believe they did an excellent job on the question of annuities and family corporations.

The situation is one that should have been taken up years ago. The injustice under it cried for relief for many years, but the minister and the Department of National Revenue felt that they were so burdened with work that they could not find a satisfactory solution and at last they arrived at the happy thought of appointing a royal commission on *the subject. AH I have to say is that a royal commission could as easily have been appointed many years previously and much less injustice would have been done many of our citizens.
Under the same caption comes resolution 2 which I will not discuss just now, but will the minister clarify the situation in regard to government annuities? At the present time government annuities taken out before a certain date are free from income tax on both capital and the income element.
Some years ago the government prevented holders of contracts that called for less than the maximum amount of $1,200 a year from increasing the amount to $1,200, which was their understanding of their right prior to that time. I believe that now, if the holder of a contract that calls for SI,200 at some future date wishes, not to enlarge his contract- because he already has a maximum-but to mature the contract at an earlier date, and he was given the understanding by the government agent-'Whether of the 'Department of Labour or of the Department of Finance is not of great concern-he could mature the contract at an earlier date and have it tax free. I see nothing in the report of the Ives commission or in the bare bones of the resolution which would throw any light on that matter and I would ask the minister to clarify it if he can.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):

speechtext:
That is a technical question for me to answer without a little notice. I shall just have, to read the question and try to answer it later.

All I can say is that the Department of National Revenue in its arbitrary manner, which perhaps it cannot help unless it gets greater clarification of the law which this house passes, rules one way at one time, and subsequently on the' same set of circumstances rules another way. Nobody knows where he stands on this matter, and before the budget resolutions are through I hope that the minister, with the assistance of his experts and his colleague, will be able to give a ruling to the people who are interested in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Surely the minister is not suggesting that dominion government annuities which are entirely tax free up to $1,200 are to be taxed as to interest element?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I did not say that. I want
to get the hon. gentleman's question clear. Is it that annuities which have been advertised as entirely free from income tax are to be free? Is that not the question? This whole matter, of
dominion government- annuities is one, which,
I may say, I was quite shocked about when the minister virtually broke the word of the dominion government in regard to them. The matter needs clarification at the present time. The annuities are sold by the Department of Labou'r, and certain representations were always made in connection with them. One was that if you took out an annuity for no matter how small the amount you could always enlarge it up to S1.200, which was the maximum, to look after your old age. The government realized that some of those contracts were improvident, particularly when taxes became very high, and they said that even though it may have been represented to you that you could enlarge it, you could not enlarge it for any more than you actually stipulated for at the time. That was the first breaking of the government's word.
Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is entirely incorrect.

The Department of
Labour did not do so, but the Department of Finance did. and you must look upon the action not only of Labour but of Finance before you find out where you are going to stand, because if the Department of Labour sells them with that understanding, namely, that the income from those annuities will be free of tax and then the law is changed by the Department of Finance, then, of course, you have two departments of the same organization working at cross-purposes, and if one will not assume the' responsibility for the other we have certainly come to a very sorry state of affairs.
, Mr. ILSLEY: The hon. gentleman says that I have broken the woid of the Dominion of Canada. I deny that.	.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I deny it most emphatically, and with a very great deal of resentment. The condition with regard to annuities was this. They were free of taxes up until June, 1940. There was no undertaking that they would always be tax free. On the other hand, what we did say was this: we recognized that if a person had parted with his money and paid for an annuity thinking that it would be tax free-
Why did he think so?
A government agency said so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just wait until I finish. We recognized that if he parted with his money and paid for an annuity we should say that the annuity which he bought' with the money he had parted with up to that time should be tax free; that we carried through. But there are all kinds of people all over the country who paid a dollar and bought an annuity, which gave them the option to increase it up to $1,200, and they just sat back, waiting until a more convenient time would come, or it would be more opportune for them to put some more money into that annuity and get it. Now there was no promise whatever by the government on the statute books, none whatever-
Not on the statute books.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

If the tax law changes in the meantime that is not breaking the word of^ anybody; that is not breaking the word of the dominion government.

I was trained in business. In business it is considered breaking one's word if one does not live up to one's contract. All the minister has said shows how

improvident the contract was. On the other hand the government did allow people to pay in $5 or $50 and obtain a piece of paper. The understanding given, not by a casual salesman but as a regular policy, I suppose in thousands of cases across the country, was that you could take out an annuity for as little as you liked and always enlarge it up to $1,200, the maximum amount allowed, whenever you could afford to do so. That was not merely always understood; that is what they were told. It is true it is not in the statute, nor is it on this piece of paper you get evidencing your contract; but it was most definitely understood by the Department of Labour and proclaimed by their agents, who, I say, are agents of the government. The government cannot deny what one department does and at the same time take advantage of it on the other hand. There is no doubt that many people who felt they had a right have had that right taken away from them. I forgive the government, if you like, for having committed that moral breach of contract, which people certainly consider it to have been. What I am asking is, where do people stand to-day with this change that is to be made in the tax law? Surely there is a contract between the government and the holders of these annuities taken out before a certain date, that such annuities will be tax free. I am asking whether or not the government intends to live up to the well understood provisions of the government annuity legislation.

The hon. member for Rosedale did not mean to say it, but he said it. What he did mean was that some agent said, "If you buy these annuities, they are tax free and you need not pay for them in full. You can pay as little as $5 or $1, if you like, and years from now you can put in some more money and that also will be tax free." In the meantime we changed the law, so that these annuities will be taxable; but where is the equity? The man has not parted with a cent. He has not denied himself the opportunity of making an alternative investment by putting his money into this annuity. Under the law as it stood at that time he could increase his annuity holding, and it would be tax free; that was his right, if he cared to exercise it. He leaves that; he does not exercise that option, because that is all it was, until after the law has been changed. Then the annuity he takes out after the change in the law is taxable. So that he has no equity at all, and under such conditions I am most surprised that the hon. member should talk about the government of Canada breaking its word.	.

Not only that, but I think if I go. back three or four years, before this became a heated issue, I could find where the minister admitted it; certainly I have always carried that impression in my mind, 47696-167
and I will see if I cannot check it. I do not say for a moment that the individual has been greatly prejudiced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should say not.

That is, not as far as anything he had himself is concerned; but he thought he had this right because the agent told him he had. Let me tell the committee exactly what happened. An agent came to an individual and said, "You can take out a government annuity, which is fax free. Put in $100, if you like." The man said, "Well, I will take one out for $100, until I am ready to enlarge it." He might just as easily have said, "I will take one for $1,200, the maximum, and here is my $100 for this year." It all depended on whether the man stipulated $1,200 or whether he said $100, thinking he always'had the right to enlarge it. Subsequently the government takes away the option to enlarge it on the same favourable terms. There is no doubt that many people who have these contracts have felt the effect of this change, as I have explained it to the minister. All I can say to him again is that while he may not like the strength of my assertion that I consider it to have been a breach of contract, no business organization that valued its name would allow its agents to make statements over a period of years, on the strength of which people purchased these annuity contracts, and then change the terms of the option.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No business company .has the right to . impose taxation. Their agents do not go around promising that their employer will never impose any taxation, or never change the taxation laws; and I am doubtful whether any agents of ours ever did that.

Certainly in connection with annuities sold by the government over a period of years the sellers of the annuities have definitely left the impression with their clients, the people of Canada, that if they participated to a degree in an annuity, the maximum they could purchase would be $1,200. There is no doubt about that. If the minister has had any discussions on annuities over the last few years, that must have been one of the salient features brought to his attention at that time. People believed it was a sort of savings account which definitely was not taxable. That was a great feature of the annuity, and that impression was left in the minds of the people.
The hon. member for Rosedale is simply saying this. When the heads of substantial corporations are confronted with a similar

264S
Income War Tax

situation, where there is the shadow of a doubt in favour of the customer, they first convince themselves of the facts of the case. That is common practice among the larger corporations on the north American continent and in other parts of the world. Then, when those facts have been substantiated and it is shown that their representatives have created an impression that has been acted upon by those purchasing a commodity, they do everything in their power to keep their good name and live up to the understanding. If the government find it necessary to pass a new law, I do not think they are in any different position from that of a private corporation. They cannot say, "We must forget all the implications that were left when these gratuities were sold, because there is a new law which governs everything and implications do not amount to anything; good will on behalf of the government does not amount to anything. We are entirely different from any other corporation that wants to stay in business." If that is the attitude of this government the result will be the same; they will last just as long as any corporation lasts that does not live up to the word of its representatives.

I should like to ask the minister if there is any particular significance in the word "contractual." After all, an annuity is an annuity. Is a contractual annuity something different? I believe that in the old income tax act there were certain annuities in connection with which some differentiation was made for taxation purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are other than contractual annuities. The annuities dealt with in the next resolution, annuities received under the provisions of a will or trust, are different.
I do not think that is a real annuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it is.
Is there any annuity that is exempted from this, and that is not covered by contractual? If so, what are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Any annual payment is an annuity. In my own mind the two classes of annuities-and I think these are the only two classes of any importance-are the annuities one buys, or contractual annuities, and annuities payable under a will or a trust document. You do not buy them. They are not contractual annuities. There may be other forms of annuities besides those, but I cannot think of them.

Before we pass this resolution I consider it important that we should discuss pretty well the capital element in annuities. 
I look upon annuities as one of the greatest sources of economic security a government can provide for its citizens. Any advantages they enjoy indeed react finally to the benefit of the nation, inasmuch as those people are not likely to become charges upon the public or the taxpayers.
I recognize, of course, that there are many forms- of annuities, and I recognize, too, what the minister has said that it may be difficult to arrive at. But in determining its course in connection with this resolution the government must have had the advantage of studying the report of certain officers and authorities, and also the benefit of having' seen the report of the royal commission.
There are annuities for certain definite and specific terms of years-ten, fifteen or twenty years. There are annuities which provide for specific periods, and' for life. There are annuities which provide for life only.
I have listened to discussion with respect to what the hon. member for Rosedale has had to say. That is to say, I have had something to do with men who mighk make promises, or lead customers to believe certain things in good faith at the time. In the main, ff this commission's report results in annuities being put on a sound actuarial basis, it will be a great advantage to the nation; because annuities have been sold in the past which were not really actuarily sound, and many wealthy people have gained advantage from buying them. By doing so, they have escaped a certain element of taxation. But unless the contract itself states specifically that they are exempt from taxation, I do not think, myself, that the government should be charged with a breach of contract.
I know that if one were to purchase with $5 or $10 an option to purchase or to increase the annuity to $1,200 a year, particularly at the rates at which they were one time sold, he would have a terrific advantage. But now that we have arrived at this stage there should be some clause written into an annuities contract so that a purchaser of an annuity will have that degree of security, and know exactly where he is at.
I can understand where someone might plan to retire, and consider that $100 a month would be sufficient to meet his retirement requirements. Then at a later date, because the law might change, and that annuity becomes subject to taxation at a greater rate, of course the amount he has provided for his advanced years might be inadequate. Therefore, rather than be too critical* of what has taken place in the past-and we might possibly be somewhat critical-I am more inclined to approach this problem from what

Income War Tax
it provides now. I think the minister should be able to tell us what factor to use in determining the capital element in contractual annuities, because, after all, annuities are more or less amortized. There is an element of interest, and one must know on what basis the interest is computed so as to return the capital sum, in relation to the number of years the annuitant is expected to live. This should not be a difficult task, whether there is a sliding scaje of guaranteed annuities for a certain specific term of years, or a sliding scale to provide for a life annuity, or annuities .that guarantee a capital return, and so on.
Therefore I feel that whatever we do now should be done with the thought that we will restore a measure of confidence to those people who might anticipate purchasing annuities. I believe that the more people who buy annuities, the better it will be for this country. As I have already said, they will never be charges on the national, in any sense of the word, but will have laid by out of their best earning years sufficient funds properly amortized to provide for the remainder of their lives. That is what I think should be clarified now-what we propose to do in the future. That is to say, shall we write into an annuity a particular amount that is subject to taxation, or otherwise, so that the purchaser of an annuity henceforth will know exactly what he has in his possession, and what its capital value will be.

To a degree I find myself in sympathy, with the remarks made by the hon. member for Grey North. I think government annuities could be covered on a different basis from some other savings effected and investments made. I believe it is an inducement to a young man or a young woman to begin saving early in life to take care of old age, and it is very often the means of relieving a community of a liability which that community would have to assume.
If we take the figures advanced by life insurance companies we find that a very large percentage of our people who reach the age of sixty-five years are dependent upon relatives, friends, or charity, and I think government annuities should be widely advertised and should have behind them the best possible salesmanship. The government should offer every inducement to young people to begin annuities early in life. That, I believe, is what the hon. -member for Grey 'North had in mind.
So far as the annuity in question is concerned, I know that last year my own daughter bought a government annuity. She was informed when she bought this annuity which 47696-1674
was payable in -later years at $50 a month, that if she felt at some time she could increase it to $1,200 a year, such would be permitted under the contract she -was signing. That, I understand, is the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
That was why I offered my interjection when the hon. -member for Rosedale was speaking: "Is that correct?" I had a hand in getting my daughter started on this particular annuity.
You can increase it.
Yes, right up to $100.

You can increase it on the same terms as you have taken the original contract. What I am complaining about is that you cannot increase the old contract, because of the change in the income tax law. The old portion of the contract originally bought is tax free, while the new portion is not tax free. If the minister will look at section 5 of the Income War Tax Act, and particularly paragraph (k), he will see evidence of the great trouble the government went to cancel all those contractual rights in this connection.

I understand that quite well. But let us look at the two cases. You have one young person who buys an annuity, and who decides to put in, we will say $10 a month for a number of years regularly. But it seems to me that the hon. -member for Rosedale is arguing from an entirely different point of view. Mr. JACKMAiN: That is right.
Mr. COLDWELL,: Let us take, for example, an insurance policy. of finding a very different sort of policy presented to me. I think that was overlooked in the remarks of my hon. friend.
I do not want to enter into any argument between the hon. member for Rosedale and the minister; that is their argument and I am not going to inject myself into it because I sometimes find that a person who does that finds himself in difficulty The more favour-

able the conditions for the purchase of annuities are made, the more encouragement That is given to people, particularly young people, to take an annuity early in life, the better it will be for our society. There may be two entirely different contracts but ultimately they have the same effect: the government gets the use of a certain sum of money. When that is spread over a long period of time it seems to me it is a valuable thing.
If the persons who buy these annuities realize that they are helping themselves, that they are assisting the country and that they have behind those annuities something which no corporation can possibly give them, that is, all the assets of the Dominion of Canada and the guarantee of this nation that at a certain period of time the annuity will bring them in a certain benefit, they will probably buy more annuities. basis, unless the Department of Finance is willing to adhere to the representations of the Department of Labour.

No base is allowed in computing income where the income of an estate is kept in hand for a certain number of years. Suppose an estate earns only $500.
